speechtext:
I lay on the table the report of the British Columbia-Yukon-Alaska Highway commission, together with the evidence.
I have a statement of the main features of the report. It might be of interest to the house to have that statement on record. If it is agreeable I ask that it be placed on Hansard. It simply sets forth the main features of the report.
Report of British Columbia-Yukon-Alaska Highway Commission (Canada)
This commission was appointed by order in council of December 22, 1938. It was instructed to inquire into the engineering, economic, financial and other aspects of a proposed highway to connect the Pacific Northwest of the United States with Alaska by way of British Columbia and the Yukon.
This project had been under consideration by various official and unofficial bodies in Canada and the United States for some twelve

Alaska Highimy Commission
years or more, and reports had been made by a United States commission in 1933 and by a Canadian interdepartmental committee in 1938. This latter report was not published. In 1938 representations were made to the Canadian government by the government of the United States with regard to the desirability of providing for the construction of such a highway, and the Canadian government was informed that the president of the United States had appointed a commission of five members ''to cooperate and communicate directly with any similar agency which may be appointed in the dominion of Canada in a study for the survey, location and construction of a highway to connect the Pacific northwest part of continental United States with British Columbia and the Yukon Territory in the Dominion of Canada and the Territory of Alaska."
In the spirit of these instructions to the United States commission by the president, the Canadian commission which also consisted of five members, was instructed by the Canadian government "To meet for the purpose of discussion and exchange of information with the United States commission appointed for that purpose."
The Canadian commission, which consists of the Hon. Charles Stewart, Major General Thomas L. Tremblay, Mr. J. M. Wardle of the Department of Mines and Resources, Mr. Arthur Dixon of the Department of Public Works of British Columbia and Mr. J. W. Spencer of Victoria, with Mr. Stewart as chairman, held a series of public meetings in British Columbia and the Yukon in the summer of 1939, and, under its direction, reconnaissance surveys were carried out by the dominion and provincial engineers, both by air and on the ground.
The substance of these hearings and surveys was communicated to the government in a preliminary report in April, 1940. The commission at that time felt that further ground work by engineers would be necessary before it would be in a position to give a reasoned opinion on the respective merits of different routes that had been proposed for a highway. These additional surveys were carried out in the summer of 1940, and when the reports of the engineers had been received the commission proceeded to consider and digest all the available information. It also, in accordance with the instructions of the order in council, held meetings from time to time with the members of the United States commission, and discussed with them various problems arising out of their respective investigations.
The commission, having completed its investigation and deliberations, prepared for the information of the government of Canada the very comprehensive report which has now been tabled. This report, after surveying the results of previous inquiries, and summarizing the evidence obtained at the public hearings, describes in detail the various routes investigated by the commission, and analyses the information collected on the natural resources of the regions traversed by various proposed routes, the character of the country, its climate, snowfall, and so forth.
The commission has embodied in its report a great deal of relevant data, including estimates of costs. The commission itself reports that either of the two main routes investigated, known as the "A" and "B" routes, is practicable from an engineering point of view. It is understood that the United States commission concurs in this conclusion.

These routes, the former nearer the sea and the latter nearer the mountains, are shown on the map accompanying the commission's report. The "A" route runs roughly from the vicinity of Fort St. James, in northern British Columbia, and by way of Atlin. near the British Columbia-Yukon border to Whitehorse, and from there to the Alaskan boundary. The "B" route from Prince George extends north through what is known as the Rocky Mountain Trench to Liard River and down the valley of the Pelly to the Yukon and from there to Dawson and the Alaskan boundary. The commission, after balancing the advantages and disadvantages of each route, concludes that the "B" route would best fulfil the purposes of the proposed highway.
In its consideration of the proposed highway the commission has assumed that the existing roads of British Columbia from the international boundary north to Prince George and Fort St. James would form part of the highway whatever route might be adopted, and confines its consideration of these existing roads to an estimate of the cost of bringing them up to the suggested standard of the highway.
The commission finds that the length of the highway from Vancouver to the Alaskan boundary would vary from about 1,700 miles to about 1,900 miles according to the route adopted.
The commission estimates the cost of a highway completed to the required standard, but exclusive of paving, at from $25,000,000 to $30,000,000, but as these figures are based upon reconnaissance surveys they are only approximate. The "B" route would be somewhat shorter than the "A" route and would cost less both to construct and to maintain.
The commission expresses its appreciation of the cordial cooperation of the government of British Columbia in placing all relevant maps and engineering data at its disposal and in authorizing at considerable expense additional field surveys by its engineers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of
privilege. In the Montreal Gazette of Wednesday, November 12, in the column written by Mr. F. C. Mears, the Gazette's parliamentary correspondent, the following statement appears:
Labour has its mouthpieces in the house, Angus Maclnnis and Clarence Gillis. The latter yesterday in the house sought to tell fellow-members that there would be trouble in the mining area if labour's demands were not heeded. Then he coolly informed them that he foretold to them what happened in Cape Breton. But Gillis was not just an innocent onlooker of the disruption of coal production in Nova Scotia. It wasn't that he feared there would be trouble down there; he was closely associated with those who caused the trouble.
But how long is the government of Canada to submit to the humiliation of having to listen to people who would have the world believe they are just onlookers, even shocked at what is happening, or assuming the role of the prophet and seer and telling fellow-Canadians they told them so.
Privilege-Mr. Gillis

I strongly resent the insinuations contained in this article, and I think the correspondent has violated his parliamentary privileges in classifying the elected representatives of the people as mouthpieces, a term which in the public mind is associated with those who specialize in the defence of criminals. I want to state emphatically that I am the mouthpiece of no one in this house. I am the elected representative of a constituency that is largely labour, and at all times I endeavour to represent my people as best I may.
With reference to the insinuation that I was a party to organizing the disruption of the mining industry of Nova Scotia, I should like to point out to the Gazette and its correspondent that this dispute was going on for two and a half months while I was attending the sittings of this house in Ottawa. Therefore I desire to make it publicly known that I had much less to do with those responsible for the slow-down in Nova Scotia than the newspaper for which the gentleman in question is writing had to do with some of the financial interests who have been responsible for the economic conditions that bring about labour disputes which to date have frequently disrupted industrial relations in Canada. It ill behooves any man who has already sold his pen to the financial jackals of St. James street to refer to any of his majesty's elected representatives as mouthpieces.

I am answering the insinuations contained in this article; and the language I am using is exactly the sort of language used by the writer of this article, who has referred to his majesty's elected representatives as mouthpieces.
In the last paragraph the writer in effect recommends to the government the suppression of any minority opinions in the house and he who thinks along these lines is not too far removed from Hitler. We endeavour to avoid industrial disputes by pointing out to the government the economic injustices that exist
among the common people. We do not set ourselves up as prophets or seers. We represent the broad masses of the people, with whom we are closely in touch in their every-day life. We intend to continue to expose the manipulations of the financiers and industrialists of this country who, if allowed, will travel the same road that was travelled by the ruling classes of other countries who are responsible for Hitler's domination of Europe to-day. If trouble develops at Kirkland Lake it will not be the responsibility of the common people in that area, but the responsibility of a small group of profit-mad mining magnates who place profits above patriotism at this time.

INTERNATIONAL SITUATION SINCE JUNE 14, 1941 [DOT]-Canada's war effort
The house again in committee of the whole, Mr. Vien in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, when the house rose last night I had completed a series of questions in the interests of national economy, more particularly with regard to the duplication of services to be found not only in the war departments, but in other departments as well.
In the form of some further queries I should like as precisely as I can to make a few more observations which to my mind are in the economic interests of Canada. I shall not refer to the work of the war expenditures committee, in deference to the Prime Minister's suggestion that that should be left until the next session- although I disagree entirely with that suggestion. At the same time I chafe under the inactivity resulting from lack of opportunity to do anything to help the general situation.
I have dealt with the matter of medical supplies and services. I come now to the hospitalization of our citizens, no matter what vocation they may be following, and I ask the administration to watch carefully that there is a minimum of duplication. When I make that request I have in mind that the government is charged with the responsibility of operating hospitals for the Department of Pensions and National Health, military hospitals, hospitals for the Department of National Defence for Air, and those for the naval 14873-275
services. I admit that these services call for specialization in taking care of patients in those different classes. At the same time we have in Canada also a considerable number of civilian hospitals recognized as class A on the north American continent. When I refer to class A hospitals I have in mind institutions which have the approval of a body known as the American College of Surgeons. Hospitals have as their objective that of being known as class A hospitals. I suggest that the policy advocated-not strongly enough, to my mind- of using, by contract or otherwise, space in the civilian hospitals, should be pursued.
I suggest that soldiers in the national defence forces who require hospitalization could be treated in civilian institutions, and the same would apply to patients from the Department of Pensions and National Health. There would be facilities in those civilian institutions to take care of all and sundry, thus obviating the expense of building new hospitals in different centres throughout Canada. That would seem to be the proper course, when hospital equipment of one kind and another is already available.
Secondly, it would be sound business, and in the interests of national economy, to canvass the possibility of extending the organizations at present giving hospital service, and make those increased facilities available to the military organizations, whether the air force or the army.
I am sorry to see the attitude of those charged with the responsibility of giving medical attention to the men in their charge. For example, depositions were given that it was difficult for the medical branch of the Department of National Defence for Air to treat men hospitalized from the army, because it was hard to become intimate, one branch with the other. The impression was left with us that it was necessary to have medical men from the Department of Pensions and National Health to look after the patients from that department, those from the Department of National Defence for Air to look after the patients from that branch of the service who were hospitalized, and in like manner those from the Department of National Defence to look after the men in khaki. I can visualize that in small centres there may be one, two, three or four set-ups of the kind. An organization of medical men looking after a hospital is a big organization. The ordinary 200-bed hospital requires a staff of fifty to take care of the different branches. It should not be said that it is difficult for a man in blue to look after a sick soldier in khaki, and we should strive to get more cooperation in that regard. Particularly it should be our aim to



The War-Mr. Harris (Danjorth)
encourage the civilian institutions to extend their services permanently, where it appears sensible to do so, and make themselves available by contract or otherwise, for the care of patients from the armed forces.
That is one point I should like to leave with the committee, in view of the fact that we are not to discuss the results of the war expenditures committee. I move from that point to another duplication which seems to be springing up in our midst, and which is not in the interests of national economy. I have in mind the question of salvage. At present there is a most competent salvage officer looking after the salvage operations of the Department of National Defence, and in like manner there is a salvage officer in the Department of National Defence for Air. The navy, following the English system, which is perhaps more than a hundred years old, have their own way of doing things. Then, in addition, the Department of National War Services handles a salvage problem. In my view there is a duplication of effort which is not in the interests of the country. There should be coordination among the different departments in respect of salvage. In his letter of December 5 the Minister of National Defence for Air made a good move when he asked an interdepartmental committee to sit around a table and thresh out some of their differences. Such coordination of effort should take place in the interim between now and the next session. It should not be delayed until the next session opens.
In the Department of National War Services are found some first-class men who are trying to do a job. Mr. Knightley, borrowed from the Department of Transport, is a man who can stir up the public imagination and public opinion as to what might be done with salvage. We know that in that organization there must be someone who can tell them what can be done with the salvaged material. Mr. Mark Cohen has been conscripted to see to the conservation of these secondary materials. He is located in the central part of Canada and is doing a really good job.
The difficulty has been that there are not enough materials in the different centres to warrant establishing an industry to convert these secondary materials into manufactured goods which can find their way on to the market. Another difficulty which has been referred to several times is the fact that quite often freight rates represent more than the value of the materials. It was disappointing to me to hear the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) say that 200 organizations had gathered salvage material to a value of $253,700, or an average of $1,270 each. That is not enough. I can point to one TMr. J. H. Harris.]
organization in Montreal which is doing that much every day, and there is a similar organization in Toronto'. However, these are both large centres of population where the problem is not as acute. I know of an organization in Quebec city which is doing at least $400 worth a day, and another one in Chatham which is doing $600 or $700 worth a day. There is still another one in Brantford doing $1,000 a day. Instead of each one of these organizations doing $1,270 a day, they should be doing ten times as much.
I do not want to be critical; I simply want to encourage these men to go further in this regard. In this connection I should like to offer a constructive suggestion for all who will read. As I said, in Chatham, Brantford, Toronto, Hamilton, Montreal and Quebec city there are industries which help to conserve these secondary materials and turn them into merchandise which is readily marketable. Large quantities of these finished products are being imported. At the present time there is a shipment in Montreal valued at $31,000 which was damaged by enemy action on its way from England. Other shipments come in from Australia. We do not object to importing from the sterling countries, but over and above these importations are the importations from the United States, and these take up United States exchange.
The constructive suggestion I have to make is that the activities of all the salvage organizations which work under the different departments of government should be coordinated. An inventory should be taken of everything available, and the industries already established should be given every encouragement. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) will come into the picture now. He knows something about the salvage operations carried on under the treasury branch. These industries already established could be encouraged. If they were willing to extend or expand their facilities to take care of everything that came to their factory the government could then consider assisting them by allowing them to write off a substantial depreciation. We should not forget that the men operating these industries would have to make a substantial capital expenditure to expand their plants. This depreciation allowance could be 25 per cent or even 33J per cent, but all returns over and above five per cent upon the capital investment might be returned to the government of Canada. This suggestion applies to the highly populated centres or areas in which an industry is operating at the present time. I might mention here that one is operating in British Columbia.
There are other places in Canada which present some difficulty because of freight

The War-Mr. Harris (Danforth)
rates. I refer to the three western provinces; Such an industry might very well be established in Moose Jaw. It would require coal, power, naphtha otherwise known as gasoline, and so on. The process is really a dry-cleaning process where gasoline is used to extract all matter which is of no value and thus place the product in condition to be finished. Fifty thousand dollars would be required for land and buildings, about $100,000 for machinery and $50,000 as working capital, a total of $200,000. Assurance would have to be given that the necessary priority orders would be given for the steel required and to permit the importation of the necessary machinery.
A similar industry could be established in the maritime provinces where at present there are no facilities to take care of these products. This plant could be established at Moncton or Sackville or Amherst at a similar cost. If $200,000 could be found in each of these places to establish such a plant, another $200,000 would be needed for the extension of plants already in existence in British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec. This would mean a total investment of about $600,000. The return on the investment by saving these products which are being wasted to-day would gross about $1,000,000 per year. Perhaps I could break up these figures.
The cost of the materials necessary to produce that $1,000,000 worth would be $500,000. This means that by salvaging this waste material we would be putting into the treasury of Canada or into the national economy an amount of $500,000. The cost of production would be about 20 per cent, or $200,000. The management would cost about five per cent, or $50,000. Interest on the investment at five per cent would be another $50,000. Depreciation charges on the fixed assets at the rate agreed upon-I suggested 33J per cent-taking the ' first asset of $500,000, would work out at about $150,000. This gives us a grand total of $950,000 on the cost side of the balance sheet versus $1,000,000 or even more on the sales side. The other five per cent or $50,000 could be taken by investors or returned to the administration. The common shareholders, those who had put up the original $500,000 or $600,000, could gamble as to whether or not they were making a few dollars for themselves.
I throw out this suggestion in order to bring it to the attention of citizens in the maritimes and the west hoping that they may see the possibilities of establishing an industry of this kind in their particular centres. What obtains in the civil life of this country with regard to salvage obtains in a greater degree in army camps. We all know that war is wasteful, and 14873-2754
that there are no facilities of any real consequence to guard against waste in the particular areas that I mention.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that we have to bring the Minister of National Defence for Air back to the chamber to-day because in common with many of us he is suffering from a bad cold. But when I make these remarks I do so in the interests of our national economy and in anticipation of the discussion which will come on the report of the war expenditures committee.
When we make inquiries into the departments, please let it be understood that we are not criticizing these men who are in uniform. We are not trying to stir up something of a political nature. I do not like to be called a politician working for politics alone while there is a war on. I have a hide like a rhinoceros and I can take it, but it is all so unnecessary, and I am sure that not one of the twenty-four members of the committee will rise and say that during all the time I have been on the war expenditures committee I have ever mentioned politics. I know that politics is the science of government and all that eyewash and humbug. But there is a war on now; let us do all we possibly can to win it. I say that these gentlemen who are sometimes called, although I do not like to hear it, members of the Penguin club or of the fraternity of brass hats, should not be almost belligerent, as one member put it, when we ask them questions pertaining to their departments or inquire into what they are doing. If I go with a group of members of parliament to Peta-wawa camp to look into the situation there and see what we can do to help out, I do not want a brigadier to say to us, "What are you doing here?" And when I say, "We want to see this camp," I do not want to have him say, "You cannot do so now. The place is not so tidy." I think members of parliament should have some freedom to move about and see conditions, with a view to helping out the situation. I say to the Minister of National War Services that when I made a humble request to get some sort of pass to permit me to pass the guard at the gate so that I could go into these camps to see if I could be of service to them-not to snoop around and find out what, was not right-I got this letter from the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham) chairman of subcommittee No. 2-and as it is not marked "personal" I might as well read it. The request had been made that we members of parliament who were members of the committee might be permitted to go and visit
The War-Mr. Pouliot

the camps and look things over with a view to carrying on our war work as best we could. This was the reply I received under date of August 9, 1941:
I discussed with Mr. Thorsou last evening your request to secure a pass that would enable you to enter certain buildings, camps, et cetera. He was of the opinion that no general pass can be secured.
I am sure that the Minister of National Defence for Air would give me a pass to go anywhere to look into anything.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Absolutely.

But we do not know what needs remedying until we are permitted to see what exists. We are not trying to dig up anything of a scandalous nature. If I happen to be in his fair city of Quebec- and I am there very often-and have a few hours on my hands, surely I do not have to wire to Ottawa to get a military pass to go and see a camp at Quebec, and the same with every member of the House of Commons who is interested in any particular subject. Surely we are the brigadiers in this brigade. Well, if we are, let us function as such.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I wish to congratulate my good friend the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) upon his constructive speech. He and my hon. friend the member for Broadview (Mr. Church) have made eloquent speeches at this session. I particularly appreciate what the hon. member who has just spoken has said, also one of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Broadview regarding the information bureau.
There is another thing which should be said from the point of view of national defence, and it concerns the mobility of our defence. The air training plan from that point of view will prove very valuable to this country by permitting airmen to go quickly from one part of the country to the other. Of course our railways are operating at full capacity, but all communications between the various parts of Canada should be improved, and I may mention particularly communications between the St. Lawrence river and the United States.
Frequently I have urged the repair or reconstruction of that section of route 2 between Riviere du Loup and Edmundston, New Brunswick, and from Madawaska to Maine, on account of the necessity of improving our communication facilities between the St. Lawrence river and the United States. We have now three main highways: the Montreal highway, what is called the Sir Wilfrid Laurier highway; the Levis-Jackman route, and the Madawaska-Riviere du Loup-Edmundston route. So important is road communication that
fMr. .T. H. Harris.]
the province of Ontario has received in past years $14,500,000 from the dominion government for the trans-Canada route, while up until last spring the province of Quebec had received only $400,000. It is only fair that the province of Quebec should have its share of the amount granted by the dominion government to the provinces for the construction of that route. Of course it may be said that expenditures have to be curtailed during the war. But this is strictly a war proposition. It is essential that we have as many avenues of communication as possible. We shall need material from the United States not only for ourselves but also for Great Britain and our allies, Russia, for instance, and we shall need many first-class highways for that purpose as well as the railways.
I regret the establishment of two military camps, one at Montmagny, thirty miles from Quebec, and one at Rimouski, a considerable distance from Quebec. It would have been much easier to establish a military camp at Riviere du Loup, where there were a number of most suitable locations. It would have served a better purpose at much less expense, and it would have been much more convenient for the boys, too.
With regard to what the hon. member for Danforth has said, I must remind the members of the government that it is not only the large cities in this country that should have something to do in connection with war industries. In the rural districts you will find men who are skilful workers, but they are not considered as tradesmen just because they do not belong to some labour union. But hon. members who live in the country know that in the rural districts there are many men who can do wonderful work with metals and woods, and they only need the opportunity to be of service. The situation is difficult for rural people to-day. Many of them have had experience which they could turn to good account in our war effort but they have not the opportunity now to do what they would like to do for their country. Some are over military age but still in good health, and they are experienced workers. I think it would be an excellent thing for this country if our industrial war effort were decentralized. That would give these men who have leisure an opportunity to take part in our war effort.
At the same time it would give an opportunity to men who work all the time in cities to enjoy a little rest from their ordinary work. Of course there should be consideration and discussion between the Department of Trade and Commerce and the various war departments before coming to that conclusion. There are very important data in the Department of

The War-Mr. Power
Trade and Commerce. Information should be obtained from there; it would prove extremely helpful to the war effort, by enabling skilled mechanics-carpenters and others-to do their share in this war effort at an age when they could not be accepted in the army. It would also give similar opportunities to young men who are not able to get into the army.
There is another thing. It is pretty difficult to establish a strict division between those who are healthy and those who are not. I understand that it is a main requirement of those who would enlist in the army that they must be healthy. That is only reasonable, because their task is hard, and they have to live under difficult conditions. But in industry also, including farming and the railways, we need many who are physically fit. I mentioned that the other day, and I will not enlarge upon it;
I just repeat it in order that hon. members may have another opportunity to think about it. What do you think of having men who have passed the military age, or who are unfit physically to be firemen on the railways, to work in the metal industry, or even in the lumber industry? That could not be always satisfactoiy.
Before concluding, may I, in mentioning another subject, quote two speeches which were made on Friday last at the opening of the war relics exhibition. They express two different points of view. One was voiced by a layman; it reads thus:
I can think of nothing more inspiring than to see these relics, in order that we may reach in ever-growing measure the conclusion that this is our war, that waiting for it to get to Montreal is the surest way to guarantee that it will come to Montreal, and that meeting it as Canadians want to meet it with everything we've got is the surest way of making certain that the kind of damage which is exemplified will not be done here.
That is one point of view, and it was expressed by a layman, Mr. Dunning. On the other hand, there was another speech made on the same occasion, by the officer commanding the military district of Montreal, which was diametrically opposed to that. He said: Menace Closer
Speaking to the French audience, Brig.-Gen. E. deB. Panet, officer commanding military district No. 4, drew attention to the reports of submarines along the east coast of Canada.
"The nazi menace is geting closer and closer to our shores", he warned.
This is a serious matter, and it is brought forward by one who has technical experience in the army. Of course, all army matters, like everything else, may be considered from the point of view of logic and common sense. The man in the street may pass his own judgment about what he finds, in any matter, not in
conformity with logic and common sense. That is why judges at times have occasion to>
decide upon such purely technical matters as electricity, although the judges themselves are far from being electricians.
That being so, I hope that the minister will take careful note of what has been said by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) and. myself regarding the establishment of industry,, and that he will take note also of the suggestions regarding the necessity of improving the mobility of our defence, and that in due course they will prove helpful to this country. We cannot wait to organize the defence of this country. There are many things lacking in many respects. I will not enumerate them, because this is not the place to do so, and I did so privately the other day. I do not want to create trouble or anything of the sort, but I want this country to be well defended, and I can point my finger to many things which are deficient. This country must not be exposed in any respect. We-all the people of Canada-must be well-protected. That is the first duty of the Department of National Defence. This is the Department of National Defence of Canada, it is not a department of international defence of the world; it is a Canadian department for the defence of Canada, and whatever we can do after that for Great Britain and other allies, we will do it with great pleasure.
I would ask the minister to be kind enough to answer the question I put to him yesterday, namely, whether the extension of the training from four months indefinitely has-been done by order in council or by the minister himself under his signature.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
If my hon. friend (Mr. Pouliot) will permit me, I will first refer to-the observations of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris). I appreciate his good-will and good intentions in saying what he did. I would be -the last to assert that any of the defence departments were above criticism; and I entirely 'agree with him that, when hon-members criticize expenditure, waste, and duplication, they are not only within their rights but are only performing the duties for which they were sent here.
With respect to the salvage question I a at fully aware that no one in this chamber is-more familiar with the matter than my hon-friend. I have always felt personally that there was a great deal of waste in all military camps or camps of a military nature. That is almost inevitable; and anything which can be done to stop that waste will be to the best general interest of Canada.
Now, with regard to visiting the camps, let me put the other side of the case to my hon-
The War-Mr. Power

friend and to this committee. Personally I feel that any hon. member should be entitled to visit the camps whenever he pleases. But we ran into this kind of difficulty. Hon. members would go to see our air training camps, or perhaps our operational aerodromes on the coast, and bring with them a party of ten or fifteen women and children. That involves an officer or more, a staff, really, at the station having to be detailed to look after them and see that they do not run into propellers, and so on. If we were always certain that the member would go by himself or with a small party, or accompanied only by persons of whom he could take full charge and responsibility, there would be much less difficulty. But we have had that kind of trouble, and the officers of the air stations particularly, where we have been up to the present and still are in a bit of a hurry to get our men out, and do not like to have the training interrupted, sometimes felt that it was perhaps a bit too much when we must detail someone to look after tourists. But as a broad general principle I entirely agree with my hon. friend that the members of this house are the representatives of the people, they have their responsibility, they should know what is going on and they should certainly have fullest permission to visit any station, any training camp, and, as far as the limits of safety permit, any of the munitions plants we have.
The hon. member for Temiscouata yesterday asked me some questions. He asked me with regard to the religious service for the Roman Catholics at Pennfield Ridge. I inquired and have a report from Rev. Monsignor Charest, the senior Roman Catholic chaplain in the air force, which I forwarded to my hon. friend personally. The sum and substance of it is that there is a shortage of Roman Catholic chaplains in that particular district, but we hope to overcome that shortage within a short time.
A further question asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata was on what authority training was extended, first from one month to four months and then from four months to an indefinite period. The hon. member said:
If he (the minister) is good enough to-morrow to tell me whether it was done by order in council, or done under the minister's signature, by virtue of the regulations, that will be sufficient.
The enabling statutory authority for the calling out of men is contained in section 2, chapter 13, statutes of Canada, 4 George VI, assented to on June 21st, 1940:
An act to confer certain powers upon the governor in council for the mobilization of natural resources in the present -war.

Section 2 reads as follows:
Subject to the provisions of section three hereof, the governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, requiring persons to place themselves, their services and their property at the disposal of His Majesty in the right of Canada, as may be deemed necessary or expedient for securing the public safety, the defence of Canada, the maintenance of public order, or the efficient prosecution of the wrar, or for maintaining supplies or services essential to the life of the community.
Section 3 of the act states:
The powers conferred by the next preceding section may not be exercised for the purpose of requiring persons to serve in the military, naval or air forces outside of Canada and the territorial waters thereof.
Under the authority of the act and under these regulations, order in council 4904 was passed on September 17, 1940, and published in the Canada Gazette on September 21,
1940.	The period of thirty days' training is referred to in clause 5 (f), which states:
Upon his being so posted to a corps of the nqn-permanent active militia, a man shall forthwith undergo training for a period of thirty days, or for such other period as the Minister of Defence may from time to time prescribe, unless he is required for service or duty. Thereafter, so long -as he remains a member of the non-permanent active militia, he shall be liable to perform such training, service or duty, but only within Canada and the territorial waters thereof, as the minister of defence may from time to time require.
It will be noted in the above and following clauses that the minister of defence is empowered not only to prescribe or amend the period of training, but also to prescribe the liability of each man so called out to perform such training service or duty as the minister may require, -within Canada and the territorial waters thereof.
By order in council P.C. 1910, dated March 18, 1941, clause 8 (f), the thirty-day period was amended as follows:
Upon so becoming a member of the active militia each "R recruit" shall forthwith undergo training for a period of four months, or for such other period as the minister of defence may from time to time prescribe, unless in the meantime he is required for service or duty.
In pursuance of the authority granted to the governor in council by the statute and of the delegation of such authority in the two orders in council referred to above, the Minister of National Defence issued the following order, which was signed at Ottawa on July 2,
1941,	and published as an appendix to Canadian Army Order No. 132 of July 10, 1941:
Requirement for service, duty or additional training in respect of men called out in pursuance of the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940.
In pursuance of the powers vested in me by Section 8 (f) of Reserve Army (Special) Regulations, 1941, as made and established by

The War-Air Services
order in council dated March 18, 1941, P.C. 1910, and amendments thereto, I, the undersigned Minister of National Defence, do hereby require all men now undergoing training in pursuance of the said seotion 8 (f), and all men who hereafter may be called out for training pursuant to the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940, and who, under and by virtue of seotion 8 (d) of the said Reserve Army (Special) Regulations, 1941, have become or will become members of the active militia, to perform service, duty or additional training on the completion of such training for which they were called out, or on the termination of any postponement of such service, duty or additional training, but only within Canada and the territorial waiters thereof, and for the period of the duration of the war existing on the 21st day of June, 1940, except when from time to time during such period I may not require them to perform such service, duty or additional training.
Dated at Ottawa, Ontario, this second day of July, A.D. 1941.
(Sgd.) J. L. Ralston,
Minister of National Defence.
Also published in Canadian army order No. 132 is the following order of the Minister of National Defence, concerning the further training, service or duty of thirty-day recruits:
Requirement for training, service or duty in respect of men called out in pursuance of the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940.
Thirty-day Recruits
In pursuance of the power vested in me by Section 5, subsection (f) of Militia (Special) Regulations 1940, as made and established by order in council dated September 17, 1940, and amendments thereto, I, the undersigned Minister of National Defence, do hereby require those men who were called out under The National Resources Mobilization Aot, 1940, being Chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada 1940, and now enrolled in the active militia, and who have undergone training under and by virtue of Militia (Special) Regulations 1940, to perform further training, service or duty m such numbers and at such times as I may from time to time require for the period of the duration of the state of war existing on the 21st day of June, 1940, but only within Canada and the territorial waters thereof, except when from time to time I may not require them to perform such training, service or duty.
Dated at Ottawa, Ontario, this 30th day of June, A.D. 1941.
(Sgd.) J. L. Ralston,
Minister of National Defence.
The Canadian army order No. 132 and appendix were approved by the war committee of the cabinet at its meeting held on April 23, 1941.

Was it published in the
Canada Gazette?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My hon. friend asked me if
I recollected by what machinery the period of training became four months. That machinery was an order in council published in
the Canada Gazette. Subsequently, under the powers conferred upon the minister in pursuance of the authority granted to the governor in council by the statute, and the delegation of such authority by the two orders in council, the minister issued an ordel which was published as a Canadian army order. I could not say offhand whether that appeared in the Canada Gazette or not.

I do not think so. The
Minister of National Defence told me that the orders are not available to hon. members, although they could get them at any bookstore. I find it very strange, because there is an order in council to the effect that each member is entitled to a French and English copy of all publications. But I am delighted that the text of the order has at last been made public. But what I cannot understand is that the principle delegatus non potest delegare has been overlooked. The government has been delegated some powers by parliament, and therefore under the militia act and the Borden act, every regulation of the kind is made by order in council. Of course the minister is in charge of the department. I find it hard to think that the minister could change by his own signature and under his own authority what has previously been decided by order in council, and though the order in council gives him a free hand-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
For service or duty. He
has always had authority under all acts to call the militia out for service or duty.

But it has been done in
a strange way, the minister will probably admit. If the principle that the delegate cannot delegate is overlooked to that extent, then the minister will be able to transfer his authority to someone else, and what will be the end of it? The only way to save the situation would be to make public, by inserting them in the Canada Gazette, all orders of the kind made by the Minister of National Defence.

Will the minister tell us how many of the 110,209 men who were serving overseas in various theatres of war as of October 25 last were in the army, how many were in the navy, and how many were in the air force? Would he tell us also, if he can, how many of those men were serving in the British isles in the various branches of the service?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The 110,209 men were all in the army. I will not tell my hon. friend how many I have in the air force overseas; I am not allowed to do so. I will not tell my hon. friend how many of the overseas men are in
The War-Air Services

the British isles, in Newfoundland or elsewhere; I am not allowed to tell him that either.
This is all the army, then?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The 110,209 men are all the army. The navy and air force are separate and apart from that.

I should like to ask the minister a question having to do with leave for trainees. As I understand the matter, when a man is called up for training the divisional board has power to grant him at least one postponement, for a period not exceeding six months. After he is called up and starts his training, however, the divisional board has no further jurisdiction; the man then comes under the military authority.
The circumstances of a man may vary greatly from the time he is called up until he completes his training. I have in mind an instance of this kind. A man may have been on a farm with his father; they were working the farm between them. During the course of his training his father dies. There is no help employed on the farm; the soldier is the only one who can take charge, but he is now under the authority not of the divisional board but of the army. In these circumstances how does he go about applying for leave? Does he apply to his commanding officer; and, if so, does the commanding officer have to forward that application to a higher authority? A further question arises: does his commanding officer or any higher authority have to regard the matter in the same rather judicial light as that in which the divisional board would examine it? Would they take into account all the facts underlying the application and give them full consideration, or would they perhaps be activated or influenced more by their desire to have another man added to their strength? Is that matter being considered?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not know whether this is simply a hypothetical case, but if it is a case of which the hon. member has knowledge I should like to ask the officers of the department to have a look at it. Broadly speaking I would say that as soon as the man is ordered by the registrar to report he comes under the jurisdiction of the army. Then so far as I know there is nothing to prevent his commanding officer from granting him compassionate leave. As to what attitude the commanding officer will take with regard to the man under his control, again that depends on the commanding officer. I see sitting opposite me the hon. member for Royal. I should say he might allow his compassionate feelings to sway his judgment; and in all
probability if he were the commanding officer in a case like this the application would be granted. I know other men who would not do that, but I think the same argument might be applied to the divisional registrar. I do not think a man would become more hard boiled just because he happened to put on a uniform. Each case would have to be judged on its merits. I am sorry I cannot give any better answer than that.

Just before the minister
rose I made a note on my pad that the man would be granted leave on compassionate grounds. That is the usual thing.
Mr. D1EFENBAKER:	Last evening I
directed a question to the minister in regard to the imposition of the national defence tax on pensions. I should like to ascertain now from the minister what is the attitude of the department.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

speechtext: They must be all in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I believe that completes the list of questions. There may have been others, but I believe they have been answered.

There is one anomaly to which I suggest consideration should be given. I have in mind the provision I have already brought to the attention of the Minister of Pensions and National Health. The provision now in effect is this: A soldier discharged prior to July 1, 1941, may make
The War-Pensions and Health

application for pension, and his application may be turned down. He may then launch an appeal, but he will receive no gratuities or assistance during the time he is awaiting the outcome of the appeal. Similar cases have now come to my attention respecting men who returned from overseas service, arrived in Canada prior to July 1, 1941, and have been discharged and denied a pension. The instance I have in mind at the -moment is that of a man resident in my own constituency who returned from overseas prior to the date mentioned, and who to-day is living in a state of destitution because he can get no assistance whatsoever. He cannot obtain relief because of the attitude of the municipal authorities, who take the view that he is a charge on the federal government.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): Is he pensionable?

His application for pension was turned down. The circumstances in connection with his case were these. He went on leave at Christmas, 1941, while in England. The pension authorities take the position that he was injured at that time. His claim is that he was injured on service on November 11, 1939, in England. He has returned to Canada, and to-day he is living in a state of destitution.
I know about the sympathetic attitude of the Minister of Pensions and National Health, but here is an arbitrary position that is doing harm to recruiting throughout my constituency. It is only one instance, but I suggest that consideration should be given by the government to the removal of that anomalous provision. Why should the date have been set as at July 1, 1941? Why should it not have been set earlier, so as to cover every possible contingency? This man cannot get work because he is unable to work, and he cannot get relief because of the attitude of the municipal authorities that he is a charge on the government of Canada. There he stays, with his wife and family, living in the town under circumstances which will constitute a detriment to recruiting, and which are most unfair to a man who tried to give his best services, but who has been returned to Canada as a result of circumstances over which he had no control.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I presume my hon. friend is referring to the case he brought to my attention yesterday. It is being thoroughly investigated.
The date of July 1, 1941, was inserted in the order in council of October 1 to make its

operation parallel with that of the Unemployment Insurance Act. That, of course, deals with a separate phase of reestablishment, in various instances.
Those awaiting decision With respect to pensions are, so long as they are in hospital, entitled to pay and allowances for their families until pensionability has been determined. This applies to the first hearing. I do not believe provision has yet been made as to pensionability while they are awaiting the second hearing. We are now considering making a provision for pay and allowances to families over a period of four months, and I believe that would meet the case mentioned by the hon. member. This, however, has not yet been approved by council.

The instance referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) brings to my mind a number of cases I have been in a position to study. I have in mind particularly one which came to my attention recently. It had to do with a soldier who enlisted in the early days of the war, went to England and came back disabled. It was impossible for him to work, because his health was completely ruined. The report shows that his request for pension was refused on the ground that his disability was caused by a defect which existed prior to enlistment. I wonder if the government and the department would study this point and consider adopting the principle that when a recruit is accepted it is presumed he is in good health. There are many cases in which the pension board refuses a pension on the ground that the disability had its origin before enlistment. I have pleaded many cases before the boards and at all times the onus of proof is upon the soldier; he must prove that he was in good health when he enlisted. The particular case I have in mind covers a soldier who told me that he was placed in category A-l. A man placed in that category should be considered to be in good health, and it would be good policy for this government, or for this country -it is not a question of party; it is something that concerns the country as a whole-to decide that as soon as a man is accepted it is presumed that he is in good health.

I want to add a word or two to what the hon. member has said. I am in full agreement with his suggestion that when a soldier enlists he should be assumed to be in good health. I have long felt that the responsibility should not be upon the returned man to prove his case when applying for pension. Nothing will do more to deter enlistments than a continuation of the treatment which has been given in many eases.

The War-Pensions and Health
It is a long time since the last great war, and quite often it is difficult for a soldier to produce sufficient evidence to support his claim. He may have lost some papers, or he may have been in poor health for years before deciding to put in a claim. Often a man was too proud to put in a claim for compensation and he goes on for years until his health is ruined and he finds himself unable to provide a living for his wife and family. In many cases men have passed on perhaps fifteen and twenty years sooner than they otherwise would.
The government should consider making a change in the treatment of returned soldiers, not only those who came back from the last war but those who will return from this war. I hope the government will carry out its announced intention of granting a cost of living bonus to the pensioners of his majesty's forces. If we are to have equality of service all down the line it is high time we realized that if the man getting $5, $6 or $7 a day is entitled to a cost of living bonus, the dependents of the man receiving only $1.30 a day should receive a similar bonus. This is only fair if we are to have equality of service and the unity of which we hear so much. If we are to have the all-out war effort we are aspiring to, we must pull in the loose ends and realize that, even though there may be strong groups or associations which do not like this idea, even though it may be politically unpopular here or there, even though there are those who say that the returned soldiers' dependents and other pensioners are getting enough now, we must look at the picture as it is. If we are to have equality of service and an all-out war effort we must give fairness in treatment and an all-out square deal to those who are winning this war.

I want to associate myself with the remarks which have just been made. I should like to have some information as to the connection there may be between men who are in the category outlined this afternoon and unemployment insurance. There seems to be an impression about that these men are to be taken care of-that is, those who are not able to establish their right to a pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have not the full tabulation under my hand, but it will be recalled that after this session convened a copy of the order in council itself, along with an explanatory memorandum, was sent to every hon. member. The basic and fundamental reason for this order in council
was to establish the principle that anyone who enlisted for overseas service would not lose as compared with the civilian who was engaged in an insured occupation. The time spent by a man in the forces will count, and there will be a contribution by the treasury. As my hon. friend will recall, benefits were also provided for occupational training, for industrial training, for university or professional training, and also for those who could not get into insured occupations. These might be termed out of work benefits. The men would be given credit for their service and would draw benefits while awaiting employment. There is a further provision in the order in council covering those who might come back from overseas and who in the opinion of those who were supervising the provisions of the order in council could be reconditioned-someone objected yesterday to the use of that word, but that is the only one that I can think of-made over again for industrial life. These men would be' given benefits while they were being reconditioned. Briefly speaking, these are the important provisions of the order in council.
I suggest to the minister that these provisions be put into effect as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They are in effect now. That is why we passed them by order in council.

Has the government considered giving special preference in the civil service to men who enlist voluntarily for overseas service as compared with those who might be conscripted for home service where there is not likely to be any fighting?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There is a preference clause in all government contracts covering ex-service men of the old war or of the present war. During the second or third day of the present session I tabled an order in council which extended the provisions of the Civil Service Act having to do with ex-service men of the great war to ex-service men of this war, with the limitation that they must have resided in Canada before enlisting in the present war.

Mr. Chairman, I hear many rumblings about me; members are asking how long this is going to continue, how long they are going to be kept here. I have been sitting here since November 3, wondering just what benefits the country and the government itself have derived from what has taken place in this house. What have we learned, I would ask, that we did not know before from the press releases furnished by the information bureau? We get them
The War-Mr. Perley

every other day or so, and incidentally I think there is a considerable waste of money there.
Frankly I think this parliament should have prorogued and we should have entered upon a new session. It would have saved all this discussion which is going on across the floor of this house and which will all be gone over again next January. As it is now, private members have no rights, no resolutions to discuss, and there are no bills before the house. True, we have the privilege of questioning members of the government, and we have had five pretty fair statements from five members of the cabinet. Some of them were quite lengthy. They gave some information, but a lot of it was in our possession already through the press releases from the information bureau.
I deem it my duty to make one or two observations on our war effort, and I shall try to be constructive. We often hear the phrase repeated, "an all-out war effort" or "a 100 per cent war effort." I believe the Canadian people are not all convinced that we are having an all-out war effort, and to prove that the Canadian people are looking for a greater effort I should like to quote from resolutions I have here. One is from a large organization in the west. In a letter which I have just received they state that they passed a resolution asking that members of parliament insist forthwith the passing of the necessary measures to place Canada on a total or all-out war effort. They go on to state what they mean by that. They mean the complete mobilization of all industry and everything else, even the intellectual resources of Canada. The Canadian Legion is already on record for an all-out war effort. Before I came to Ottawa this session I was put on the spot by the branch of the Canadian Legion in my constituency, and I did not hesitate to agree with some of the things which they advocate should be done in order to have an all-out war effort in Canada.
Let me review our war effort as I see it as a lay member, so to speak. Since we entered the war in 1939, our war effort has developed in three phases. The first two years of the war were the development period. We were building factories, developing plant capacity. That required a lot of men, a lot of work, a lot of complicated machinery and tools. We now have these factories, some of which have received large financial assistance from the government, running in the aggregate into hundreds of millions of dollars. These plants are all interlocked, so to speak. Not one of them is producing a complete tank or aeroplane, for instance, but is engaged in manufacturing component parts. They are all
[Mr. Power.
interlocked, and as I said a moment ago, the government has contributed to their establishment hundreds of millions of dollars. There may have been mistakes made and waste in many instances. We had a committee of this house set up to inquire into government expenditures. I shall not comment upon its report, but it is only fair to say that under no government could all this development work have been done without mistakes and some waste. It is the duty of parliament and of the government now to tighten up on waste. That was the development phase.
The second phase is production. It is now necessary for the government to see that all these factories engaged on war work click, work in unison, work together as a unit. I have heard rumblings as to what is going on, that there is not the unison there might be. It is the duty of the government to see that these war plants click. The Minister of Munitions and Supply referred to that matter the other day. He said that the production of one gun or one tank might take one month, that in the second or third month six might be produced, in the fourth or fifth month, thirty-six, and I believe we have now reached the stage where we might produce 336 in a month if the government would see that these plants are clicking.
The third phase is the output of materials and a system of priorities. Tremendous production capacity has been provided. I think it is only fair to the government to say that. But now it is up to the government to see that the materials required are provided. I have in my hand a little pamphlet entitled, "Priorities and Controls in Canada" which I think it would be well for every hon. member to read. We are now at the stage where there is a strain on the capacity of the organizations which are producing materials such as steel, brass and copper. We are now in this third phase, producing the materials which are necessary. But we must have coordination so that one plant will not hold another one up.
Since the start of the war training schools have been set up. I think that is right, and a great deal of good work has been done by the schools. The men are now ready to come out of these training schools and go into factories wherever they may be required. I believe it is the duty of the government to enrol and train more men in these training schools. But the government also has a responsibility to see to the proper distribution of these men.
At this stage surely there should be no more strikes in Canada. We are at war; it is a very serious war, and strikes should not be permitted to interfere with our war effort.

The War-Mr. Perley
Since the war broke out, we of the opposition in this house have been responsible to a considerable degree in bringing our war effort up to its present stage, by pepping up the government, jacking them up by constructive criticism. At the very outset of the war our leader said that as far as he and the group he represents were concerned we would support the war effort at all times and give constructive, helpful criticism, and I believe that considerable credit for what has been accomplished is due to the opposition and the constructive suggestions they have offered1.
Why don't you keep your good leader? We all like him.

The hon. member can speak after I have finished. I have said very little during the last two weeks, and I am trying to suggest something that might be helpful to the government and its war effort.
From what we have heard from different ministers, there has been a shortage of recruits for the armed forces. Men are not available. By all military authorities whom I have heard or have seen quoted it is agreed, I believe, that we must have more men in the forces both to attack and to hold the ground after the attack. Those who have had the opportunity and privilege of going overseas and seeing what is going on there say that men are needed. All of them may not have said so publicly; there is a lot of secrecy in connection with this business: maybe the delegation which is now on its way back will have something more to tell us.
It is the government's responsibility to protect the projects which they have assisted, the factories and industrial organizations which they have helped to bring to the point of production, by providing them with the men needed to do the job in the factories. The other important job is to provide for the needs of the armed forces. I believe there are enough men in Canada to take care of both, but the situation now is rather like this, that if ten men who are roaming the streets have it put up to them that there are two great jobs to be done, what is going to happen if all of them say, "We will go into the army", or if they all say, "We will go into industrial plants to make good wages"? I say, therefore, that it is up to the government to protect both these two great activities by seeing that there is a proper distribution of men.
That brings me to the point that I think there must be some plan and some direction given by the government. Those men who are not now in the forces or even in the trainees' camps must have direction. Let me
illustrate. There is Mr. Jones out in Saskatchewan; he is a farmer and he has a crop to take off; he has five or six new binders, and there are five or six men for the job. Suppose he had not the power of direction, to say to the six men, "Get on these six binders and complete the job". The men might say, "Oh, the heck with it"; perhaps three would say, "We are not going to get on the binders," and the others might decide that they would wait for the threshing season, or one or two might make up their minds to wait until the farmer was trucking it out, because that is where the money is. If he were without power of direction to put the six men to work at the right spot, the crop would be ruined, perhaps by snowstorms-we have had a lot of them this fall. But if he had the power to say, "You get on to that job", the job would be completed properly and in time. I say that that is what the government should do now. They have the power. To my mind the only way in which it can be done is by a system of selective national service.
We have arrived at the point that the government have the responsibility to protect the industries which they have assisted with millions of money and which are now tooled up and ready to go. They are the only ones who can give the direction we need in Canada to-day. I for one do not care how it is done, or whether it is done by this government or some other government. This is the suggestion that I have to make: use selective national service and get to work on the job.

It seems to me that in the last little while we have wandered a long way from the Department of National Defence. Is the minister now in a position to answer questions in his capacity of minister for air? If he is, I would recall the statement which he made the other day, when, speaking in this chamber, he mentioned the unconditional nature of enlistment in the Royal Canadian Air Force, and referred to the fact that all those who enlisted in the Royal Canadian Air Force enlisted for service wherever they were sent. Would he care to expand that statement a little bit about the liability of ground crews, and many others in the service, for service anywhere? I do not think that is generally understood.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In the air force there is not any such thing as enlisting for home defence or for the defence of Canada. Just by way of digression, at one time there was a suggestion that certain Free Frenchmen would like to enlist on the condition that they should not fight against their own country. I did
The War-Mr. Ross. (St. Paul's)

not think that was advisable. I said that if they enlisted in the Royal Canadian Air Force they would go wherever they were told and fight wherever they were asked to fight. I can quite understand their feelings in the matter, and I do not think those who did feel like enlisting were deterred by that reply.
Some time last summer it was decided that, instead of sending overseas only aircrew, that is those who man the aircraft on actual operations, we would also send over a number of men to carry on ground duties, to maintain the aircraft and do work as aero-engine mechanics and all the various duties that go with the care and maintenance of aeroplanes. We have been sending such men overseas and shall continue to do so. In view of the number of our squadrons overseas, I expect that before long there will be several thousand ground crew also over there, and any one in the Royal Canadian Air Force, in any one of the categories, is liable to be called upon to go overseas at any time.

I should like to make a few remarks at this time. The city of Toronto is in military district No. 2, and a number of regiments are there. One battery of artillery is being formed by our famous former manager of the hockey team, Connie Smythe, and he is doing a magnificent job, but he is finding it very difficult to get men. Great efforts are being put forward to get recruits, and many people are helping, but the thing which disturbs me more than anything else is, what will happen when we cannot get them? Yesterday I listened with great interest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he made his statement to the House of Commons, and I was very much disappointed at his closing remarks, when, speaking of conscription for overseas service, he said:
So far as I am concerned, without any consultation of the people on that subject, I do not intend to take the responsibility of supporting any policy of conscription for service overseas.
The Prime Minister has told us that he has a mandate from the people to lead this country during war time. He has told us that we must fight an all-out war and that we must have an all-out effort. The Prime Minister must take the full responsibility for fighting this all-out war and exerting this all-out effort. He must take such steps from day to day, even from hour to hour, as may be necessary for the safety of the state. Now is the time for the Prime Minister to lead this country in the light of all the information which he has and the information which he has obtained from the Prime Minister of Great Britain and

from Mr. Roosevelt. The members of this house should in some way be enlightened as to what information he has so that we can understand why he still takes the stand he does. Does the mother of parliaments not have closed sessions every three or four weeks where information is disclosed to the members? Is it not better and more helpful if such information is disclosed to the members of the house? We are in dire peril these days; I think the Prime Minister knows that. We ought to be told how dire the peril is. We know what Hitler proposed to do; we know how he has carried out his plan. Do we believe it?
The defence of Britain is the defence of Canada, and our Canadian soldiers are taking part in that defence. We cannot let them down. How can a population of forty to fifty million people provide the men for ultimate victory? That is the population which Great Britain has to draw on. The combined efforts of all the nations of the commonwealth as well as all the democracies of the world are going to be needed to do this job. We must do our part. It is not a party matter; it is not a political matter; it is a national life and death struggle. The Prime Minister must put into force fearlessly and regardless of criticism and of party those policies which will be best for the preservation of Canada, knowing full well that the Canadian people and this parliament will back him up.
He has been urged from time to time to form a national government, but has refused and has given his reasons. He has taken into his non-parliamentary ranks many prominent men of varying and non-political views, and a certain amount of satisfaction has been obtained from that. The public have been satisfied to a certain extent. But party lines are different now. Old differences such as tariffs, et cetera, mean little to-day. The major differences can be only between those who are for an all-out war effort and those who are not. The knowledge of the truth will come to all eventually, but if the Prime Minister waits for it to come to all before acting, it may be too late.
Are there any who still disbelieve Hitler's programme laid down in Mein Kampjf Many thought he was a mad fool in 1936, 1937, 1938, even up to 1939, but he put into practice the plan set down in his book. The conquest of Poland, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Holland, Belgium, France, Norway, Yugoslavia, Greece, Roumania, almost all on time. It is true his time-table was held up by the valiant Poles and Greeks and some of the others to a certain extent. The Russians are doing the job now, and we cannot let them down.

The War-Mr. Casgrain
I ask the question, who comes next? There is no doubt he will attempt an invasion of England. It will fail. Then the forces of right, including those of Canada, must be prepared to invade Hitler's domain, fight him to a finish and smash him once and for all. We must prepare now. Mr. Churchill yesterday told us that by 1943 we shall be able to invade the continent. We must be ready. What is the alternative, if we do not go on and smash this man Hitler? The axe will hang over our heads until it is done. Are we not in the same position as Great Britain? Are we to be outdone by that great, indomitable leader, Winston Churchill? He said:
If the battle is to be won we must provide our men with ever-increasing quantities of weapons and ammunition. We must have quickly more aeroplanes, more tanks, guns, shells. There is imperious need for these vital munitions, and then in the emergency we shall not hesitate to take every step, even the most drastic, to call forth from our people the last ounce, the last inch of effort of which we are capable.
The interest of property, the hours of labour, are nothing compared with the struggle for life and honour, for right and freedom, to which we have vowed ourselves.
Have we not vowed ourselves to the same principles? Are our interests any different? I say now that we as Canadians must not hesitate; that the Prime Minister can and should lead this country and that the people will follow him, regardless of how drastic the action required. There has been no hesitation on the part of the government in bringing in drastic legislation, in fact revolutionary legislation, by order in council. I have no doubt that the people would have accepted this legislation perhaps a little better than they have-they have accepted it very well, but it would have been better to bring it in as legislation on the floor of the house so that it could be discussed. There might be useful information brought out and possibly a few changes made.
There must be equality of sacrifice and service in this mobilization of our full human and material resources for whatever eventuality, each man in his right place. The welfare and safety of Canadians, of the British commonwealth of nations, yes, of the whole world, are at stake. This must override our traditional individual choice of action.
I have hesitated to speak before, feeling that the Prime Minister, by reason of his words spoken so often in his appeals to the people that he intended to have a total effort, that we must have a total effort, must fight a total war, would, when the time came, make good these words with action. T cannot say
how disappointed I am that the Prime Minister is not willing to take the full responsibility for this total effort, as he told us yesterday.

speakeroldname: Hon. PIERRE FRANCOIS CASGRAIN (Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
