Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to take part in this debate, but after listening to some of the speeches that have been delivered by hon. gentlemen opposite I feel it my duty to express my views to this parliament and the country.
A great many members of this House of Commons are advocating a total war effort and are seeking, both within and without this house, to promote the idea of conscription for service overseas. Let them not contradict me; that is what they want. We are in this parliament as representatives of the people of this country. During the campaign preceding the last general election the Canadian people were made acquainted with the aims and aspirations of every party. At that time the people of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific were told that no party, including the Liberal and Conservative parties, was in favour of conscription for service overseas. Therefore the mandate given the Liberal party to govern the affairs of the country during this war was given on the principle of voluntary service. Parliament has no mandate to change this policy now without consulting the people. Canadians have not changed their minds; they still approve the present programme of the government. There have been several byelections throughout the country, at which Liberal candidates have been elected by large majorities, which proves that the policy of this government still has the support of the people. At the last by-election held in Alberta the hon. member for Edmonton East received a real mandate from the people of that constituency; and her campaign was conducted on the slogan, "No graft and no partisanship." That showed a real approval of the actions and policies of this government.
Hon. gentlemen opposite now seem to want compulsory enlistment for overseas service. I say the great majority of the Canadian people do not want it, and I know the vast majority of the population of the province from which I come are against it. The other day I listened with great attention to the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), who referred to the absence from this house of the right hon. leader of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, the gallant hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), who at present is ill, and also to the absence of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), who is away for the same reason. I am not
The War-Mr. Casgrain

going to try to speak for those hon. gentlemen, but I am going to speak as one representing the province of Quebec. I can say that the entire population of that province is as one in supporting the policies of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The feeling of the province of Quebec is that we should follow the provisions of the mobilization act that was adopted about a year ago; and my compatriots in Quebec are ready to serve anywhere from the Atlantic to the Pacific in the defence of our country, which is a sacred duty and obligation which all decent Canadians understand. Up to the present that mobilization act has done all that it was expected to do; according to the speeches of the ministers of defence, within the last six months 105,773 men enlisted in the army, the navy and air force, which I think is a very good record. In addition we have some 110,000 of our compatriots serving in England, ready to go into action whenever their services may be required. The right hon. Prime Minister was in England only recently; he saw our men over there and has reported, as has been stated in the press throughout Canada, that at the present time there is no body of men in England better equipped than the Canadian corps. At the time of Dunkirk in 1940 the only corps in England equipped and ready to face the enemy was the Canadian corps.
These are facts of which we should be proud. Under the policies of the present government, since the beginning of the war we have been able to bring about these results and it has been made known throughout the world that Canada is doing its full share and will continue to do so. Under the mobilization act the government has at its disposal adequate forces for the defence of the country, wherever they may be required and provision has been made whereby those who of their own free will wish to serve overseas, for the defence of the empire at large, are permitted to do so.
Before it could be agreed that the statements of hon. gentlemen opposite were true and ought to be considered seriously, it would have to be shown that the mobilization act and the laws of the land had not brought about the results which were expected. Far from that being the situation, I say, and I do not believe I can be contradicted, that at the present time we have in England an army consisting of four divisions and one tank brigade. With all the Canadians who have enlisted in the air force, the navy and the other services, I believe we have about twelve divisions compared with the four divisions we had in the last war. I think that is a brilliant record, of which we should all be proud.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman cannot say we have twelve divisions, if he knows what a division is.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is another point
I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members. Sometimes people wish to make it seem that the province from which I come has not done its full share. I do not say that these people point directly at us and single us out, but they claim that if recruiting is not as active as they would like it, that has been due to lack of interest in the affairs of the country and because our people have not done what they should. I wish to say most emphatically that the people of Quebec have responded to the call to the best of their ability; and if some changes had been made and improvements brought about, the response would have been even better. Only yesterday I read in one of the Ottawa newspapers a letter signed by a former member of this house, Mrs. George Black, who said:
With extreme regret, as well as great annoyance, I have noted a growing habit of accusing Quebec of lack of loyalty to Canada and the empire, because of an aversion to compulsory military service.
Probably no member of parliament, with his wife, does of necessity cover more of Canada from the far north to the east than do George Black, M.P. for Yukon, and I. In our many trips across Canada, we have observed as much apathy and lack of enthusiasm for active service in the armed forces of Canada in other provinces as in Quebec.
Let us of the other parts of this dominion forget our smug complacency and force ourselves to realize that Quebec is as loyal as the other provinces.
We are component parts of a great empire. Let each one do his, or her, part to unite Canada in support of that empire, forgetting petty racial and religious prejudices. We must work, we must fight for the right to worship one God, to be loyal to one king, and to hold a united empire, that our children's children may enjoy the freedom we hold so dear.
There is a great deal in this letter over which some hon. members in the house, and other people outside, should ponder. I do not wish to carry on this debate much longer. We have heard in the house many speeches from quarters directly opposite the government. They have pointed out that the government has been lagging and derelict in its duty. I want to ask hon. members if there was foundation for any of those criticisms.
The government of the present Prime Minister has at all times been able to handle the situation with one thing in view, that of maintaining unity in this country-unity of the various races in Canada. Without that we would not be able to carry on this war. I do not wish to attribute motives to any other

The War-Mr. Rowe
persons, but some who are facing me to-day, and others in other parts of the country, are carrying on certain propaganda in the press. I say to them, and to all those who hold such views, to consider that they are not giving good service to the Canadian people and the empire at large.
In all the provinces of Canada are to be found peoples of various races, creeds and religions. It is the aim of the country to keep all those various elements united together in order that we may present a united front, and be able to carry the burdens of the day and to give to this dominion of ours and to the empire the greatest service possible. It is helping the empire to defeat Hitler, and that is the aim of this country. It is the aim of this government, and it is the aim of all British countries.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with considerable interest to the Secretary of State (Mr. Casgrain). I, like him, do not rise more often than many other hon. members who have not been here as long as the minister or myself. WTith much of what he has said I can agree. I join with him in wishing for this country national unity of the highest order. There is no greater purpose that any member of the house, or any elector in the country, can have than that of national unity.
But, Mr. Chairman, may I draw your attention to the fact that consideration must be given to a great section of this country if we are going to maintain the necessary unity, and bring about that all-out war effort about which we are all talking. I have every respect for the hon. member who has just taken his seat. He and I have sat in the house for many years. I know he bespeaks at least the feeling of those who elected him. But when he speaks of pre-election pledges, may I point out to him that I am not going to indulge in them to-day, because he knows them better than I-and I know them better than I am going to tell the committee now.
I do not believe that to-day this government has a mandate from the people of Canada for many of the things it is doing. It is all very well to say that it has no mandate for selective conscription; but when I hear the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) on the one hand, saying that we are out for an all-out war effort; that the Canadian front is on the English channel, and that the defence of Canada is over there, and when I hear on the other side someone saying that he has election pledges, and that we cannot have selective service for overseas, but that we will adopt conscription or compulsory service for Canada, then I begin to wonder
where the front line really is. This government has inaugurated conscription. Did they tell the electors of Quebec or of Ontario that they were going to inaugurate conscription? Did they say to the farmer boys throughout the country that they would take them off the farm, whether their fathers were ill or their mothers in hospital, whether the farm went idle, or whether they had to have auction sales? No-silence gives consent.
My hon. friend who once followed the views of the farmers in another part of the house, did not talk that way. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) did not talk that way, when he was travelling down the middle of the road looking for votes. The-Secretary of State did not tell the electors that, when he visited Ontario, nor did the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), who is very popular wherever he goes. Yes, there are many things they did not tell. But I am not going to take time to refer to some of the things the minister did tell the electors throughout Quebec. I have too deep a conviction respecting my own responsibilities in the house, and yours, Mr. Chairman, and this parliament's, in this time of terrible crisis.
I am not going to stir up dangerous issues, but I was surprised by the statement made by the Prime Minister last night. I think he went only far enough in that regard to leave us where we are. But I do say that this government has no more mandate to conscript the boys of this country for home defence than it has a mandate for selective service where the Minister of National Defence says the front line is, namely, on the shores of Great Britain.
A hundred and eighty to forty.

That is all my hon. friends can think about-elections, elections. They are fearful of another election, and boasting still about the last one. They are playing politics, just as Nero fiddled while Rome burned. Let me say to them that they cannot blow hot and cold on this great issue.
Yet the Minister of National Defence says that the defence of Canada is overseas, and someone else rises in his place and says, "We will conscript men only for the defence of Canada." From the same government someone else says, "We have no mandate for conscription". Then, on the other side of the picture someone says, "We have a mandate for this form of compulsory service in our dominion". In other words, they say, "We will not tell the electors we would compel anyone to join the army, but after the election
The War-Mr. Rowe

is over we will compel the men to join the army-not where there is going to be any fighting, not where the Minister of National Defence says the danger is. We will not take a chance and give it further effect without going back for a political squabble in the country."
Let us face the facts. I believe the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) said this afternoon that it was almost unnecessary to be here, and that he would like to get away. I think he is right. I wonder now why we came here. The newspapers of this country have been filled to overflowing with legislation passed by orders in council. The newspapers suggested there would be legislation when we came here, but when we arrive we find the order paper has nothing on it but a few unanswered questions and a few discarded resolutions. Talk about depending upon the people-why, this government has scarcely depended upon parliament.
I have sat in the house and listened to the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and other hon. members, condemning the Bennett government for legislating by order in council, condemning them for issuing blank cheques, and talking about dictatorship through order in council. Never since confederation has a government passed more orders in council than the present one.
I do not wish to be unfair to the Prime Minister, because he is carrying a terrible load. Yes, he is carrying a load heavier than he would have to carry if he would take parliament into his confidence. He is carrying a heavier load than he would have to carry if he took the country into his confidence.
I make no apologies for my own party. We hear much talk about a mandate, but neither party knew in 1939 what was going to happen. Billboards were put up all across this country when we were both seeking election. We had a similar policy on this issue as those who sit to your right, Mr. Chairman, we stated that there would be no conscription. But we are now in a crisis; we are in the midst of the flash and flame of the greatest peril this country has ever faced. An hon. member says that the government has the support of 180 members. I plead, then, with the Prime Minister of this country to face these facts that confront us. We are facing the greatest peril the British empire has ever faced. There are 180 members behind him, so surely he will have sufficient-I shall not say courage -confidence to go ahead; surely he will not be afraid.
Afraid of what?
Afraid of the ballot box; that is what hon. members opposite are afraid of.
They will not need to come back by acclamation.
I have come back far more often than my hon. friend, even by election.
The hon. member has a long way to go.

This government is putting into force many orders in council. It has a right to do that in many instances because no government could face the problems that this government must face without passing orders in council. The Prime Minister and his cabinet have passed many orders in council which we all know were necessary to meet emergencies, but they have also passed many that were not necessary, especially while parliament was sitting. For instance, we had the price control or price ceiling legislation which we have heard about and which is not yet in effect.
I urge the government to take this house into its confidence. This cannot be classified as emergency legislation. This is the forum where these propositions and proposals should be dealt with. They should be brought here no matter how badly money is needed in the treasury. We met last spring; we met again this fall and yet we read about more legislation in the newspapers than we hear about on the floor of this chamber. We ask, but I have before me a list of unanswered questions. There are also on the order paper a number of discarded resolutions. These have not been reached no matter from what corner of the house they may have come. To my mind this parliament has been made an absolute mockery, more so than at any time since confederation.
The time has come when this government should take vigorous action. I should like to see the Prime Minister of this country provide by order in council for compulsory selective service and then come back to parliament and say, "I did not have a mandate to pass compulsory selective service for home service, let alone a mandate to send the boys overseas, but this is what I have done." I should like him to tell us that he had gone down to the compatriots of the Secretary of State in the province of Quebec and explained to those loyal people that the home front for the defence of Canada was overseas, that without a mandate he had brought in compulsory selective service to defend the shores of Canada and he therefore had provided for compulsory selective service for where the fighting is going to be.
Do not dodge the issue. If there is anything I can do to help this government, I am ready to do it. I have endeavoured, privately and otherwise, to make suggestions and offer

The War-Mr. Rowe
proposals to this government which I believed might help. Surely we can get away from politics for a while. Talk about national unity-
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says, "hear, hear." Nobody has played politics in Canada with greater success during the last quarter of a century than has my hon. friend. No other hon. member has been better recompensed for it either. This war far transcends any of our personal ambitions.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Essex East says, "hear, hear." The front line of this country is overseas; Canada must be defended where Hitler is charging, and not upon the banks of the St. Lawrence. We have had a compulsory service which takes boys from the farms and leaves only old men to work them. I have heard hon. members to my left refer to that and to the many auction sales which have taken place because boys from the farm have been compelled to serve in defence of Canada. This service is supposed to be here in Canada, but when the boy gets in the army he finds he is bludgeoned into joining up for service overseas. He suffers humiliation and embarrassment and feels that if he does not enlist he will be like those to whom the Prime Minister referred in western Canada. To my mind this is a shameful and-I shall not use the other term I had in mind because I believe "shameful" and "cowardly" are both unparliamentary-it certainly is an inadequate and unjust means of serving the purpose which every member of the government has said must be served.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) says that this is an all-out war, and that we must have from the people dollars and more dollars. I have endeavoured to cooperate with him in every way in order that more war savings stamps and victory bonds may be sold. I say to the government that this tremendous task is their obligation. I know their purpose is to keep prices at a reasonable level in order that there may be a basis upon which they can collect this enormous volume of money which is going to be necessary to meet the most gigantic conflict in the history of civilization. I ask hon. members to pause for a moment and compare the task of to-day with the task of the last great war. Canada is not the country she was in 1914. She is not as advanced as she might have been, but she is a stronger and greater country in both materials and man-power.

And as far as
government is concerned.

My hon. friend says, "and as far as government is cone -ned." He that complies against his will is of the same opinion still. I know my hon. friend feels quite keenly about this. While he may appear humorous in the midst of adversity, I know that when he pauses in the silence of the night he will ask himself the question: Why have we compulsory sendee to defend our shores where there is no fighting and yet no compulsory service to defend our shores where our only defence lies? Think it over. We speak about national unity, but I see no reason why we should have disunity in this country on this issue. If there is reason why we should have disunity on this issue, it is not on account of the great French people of the province of Quebec, those people who were the earliest settlers of this dominion, those loyal, conscientious people who sent thousands of sons to the last great war.
The Liberal party has played politics with this most dangerous issue. I plead with them not to play politics again in this grave hour, but to go to the people of that great province, many of whom bear upon their breasts decorations from the last great war and many more of whom will be decorated overseas in this conflict; let the leaders of this government go to the people of the province of Quebec and say, "You people who were in this country first, and who love Canada, you who know that our most sacred freedoms were achieved under the union jack, we ask you to join us now in protecting not only the shores of the Dominion of Canada but the very shores of our freedom, the shores of Christian liberty, the shores of every right we have enjoyed for so long." If the government will do that, I ask the people of this country who are harping so much on unity to say whether such an appeal would not unite other great forces in this country, and who can doubt that the great province of Quebec would march on with all of us together?
There is and has been for many years another vital part of the defence of Canada-the British navy. The United States of America realizes that very keenly to-day, and we can unite with this great force with greater hope of success than we can ever hope to achieve by standing alone until Hitler takes us one by one.
It is all very well to say that we are going to have our men employed in their proper place, that we are going to produce aeroplanes and tanks. It is not so long ago that we were told we could not produce tanks in this country, but to-day we are producing tanks, aeroplanes, and guns, and our war industries are humming all across this country, playing the game and doing their best. The challenge is up to the government to work along with them.
The War-Mr. Rowe

Name a national coordinator, if you will, who will cut the red tape that is strangling our war effort at the present time, who shall also rip off the strait-jackets from these dollar-a-year men and let them go to work. We are facing the greatest crisis in our history, and before I conclude I would urge this proposal upon the government. I do so now because this is about the only chance we get to debate issues of vital importance. All we can do, the way this government carries on the administration of the country, without consulting parliament, is either to express our thoughts in advance or to criticize after action has been taken by order in council. Otherwise we come back to parliament and find that all we can do is to criticize what has been passed. Therefore, before we leave we had better anticipate the new orders in council that will be passed after we go home. We do not know whether the government in its price-fixing policy will take fifteen cents off eggs and add two dollars a hundredweight to bacon, or add fifteen cents to the price of eggs and take two dollars a hundredweight off bacon. Even when parliament is sitting, orders in council are passed regulating these things under this new-fangled economy.
Let me warn this government, which will be rapidly passing orders in council in connection with this new-born system, that they beware lest they defeat the purpose for which it was created. Let the government ask themselves in fixing prices of farm products to be as sure of the costs of production as they are of the manufacturing costs of industry, which gets its costs, plus ten or fifteen per cent. Let the government ask themselves whether it is fair to fix prices on the same basis for industry and the farmer, who cannot pay off his mortgage or meet his bank overdraft, and who works longer hours for less money, while labour in industry works shorter hours for more money.
Think of the farmer in the cost of living bonus plan. No one has been stronger than I for the man who toils at a machine. No one has worked harder and spent more, politically and otherwise, than I have done to see that labour gets a square deal, and I still stand by labour. But in this price-fixing scheme I urge the Minister of Finance, who probably has not worked the long hours some farmers have, to pause for a moment and ask himself if he should fix prices for the farmer who is working twelve and fourteen hours a day, on the same basis as he fixes prices for industry working eight hours a day.
I urge the government-and I am giving advice that may have little effect-to take into the cabinet, in the interests of our war effort, more men who understand the problems

of labour and agriculture, just as the government of Great Britain has done, and I say that without intending any reflection on any member of the cabinet. If you want to unite this country, have all elements in our country properly represented in the cabinet, and then tell the country what needs to be done. Tell the country that winning this war is not going to be an easy matter, that this government has a job to do, and that if it fails to do it, history will hold it forever responsible. If our empire's history is to be brightened by Canada's contribution as it was in the last war, not only must we stand united, but we must march on together to the end. There are more critical days ahead, and it is the duty of the government to spur the people of this country on to greater effort. Do not pause to ask yourselves whether you have a mandate to do what the situation demands, because nobody is going to bother you even if you go a little further than your mandate to carry out an all-out war effort. Do not think so much about mandates, and politics. Think about the challenge that faces you to-day. Think of the return of freedom and liberty to the enslaved countries of Europe, which depends so much on the efforts of Canada, the richest country in the empire, the country that is attracting the eyes of the world to-day, a country that our great neighbour to the south is watching. The United States have compulsory selective service even before they are at war. Let the government concentrate on the crisis that is facing us to-day and ask themselves whether they can afford to play politics as it has been played in normal times.

I am not sure whether I heard the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe (Mr. Rowe) aright, but I understood him to say that our war effort was being hampered by red tape. Those were not his exact words, but that is the substance of what he said. That certainly is not true or fair. I have in my hand a pamphlet containing an address given by a member of this house in the last parliament, Mr. J. A. Marsh. He was a defeated candidate in the last election and now occupies an honoured position in the Department of Munitions and Supply, where he is engaged in the examination of contracts. In this address he says, "There is no political patronage in the Department of Munitions and Supply."

I think there is just enough time before six o'clock for me to say what I desire to say. My voice is not quite so loud as that of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe; my frame is not

The War-Mr. Hansell
quite so large; but I trust that my logic is
as sound; and anything that I say now I do not say in defence of the Liberal party.
I agree with the sentiment which has been expressed that in the last general election the people of this country were under the impression that by voting Liberal we would not have conscription. I have searched records;
I have gone back over newspaper articles, and I cannot find that anywhere any mention was made of or any distinction drawn between, overseas service and home defence; and the people themselves voted at the last election against any kind of conscription.
Coming to my hon. friend's remarks, I fail to understand how our Conservative friends could have changed their minds so quickly. The fact of the matter is that we have not heard very much about this conscription business until the last few days.
Has the war changed since then?

The war has not changed in the last few days; but supposing it had, I will come to that in a moment. In the last election, about eighteen months ago, this group which I represent made their stand definitely clear. They had the foresight to anticipate that we would have a long, hard battle and that the time might come when the entire resources of the dominion would have to be brought into the war effort. Our stand then was: begin the right way, by mobilizing the financial resources or-should I say?-the financial institutions of this country, that the government might take unto themselves that which they had delegated to the financial institutions and control the credit facilities of this country to aid in the war. That, we said, was the first thing to do. We went out on the platform in the election and said the same thing. Did our Conservative friends advocate conscription at all in those days? They did not go even as far as we did. But now, in the last few days, there suddenly springs into existence a cry by these hon. gentlemen for some type of conscription.
They do not say even yet what they want.

To-night's paper has a rather large headline:
Arthur Meighen accepts leadership of Conservative party.
To urge compulsory service over whole field of war.
I suppose that means foreign service as well as home service. We did not hear anything about that eighteen months ago. One can come to only one of two conclusions: either
my hon. friends are indulging in political opportunism by grasping at what may be regarded in some opinionated circles as a growing public sentiment over the subject of conscription, or, they were not far-sighted enough to see what might happen eighteen months afterwards. For a party to bid for power that cannot see eighteen months ahead is-well, I would not vote for them anyway. I do not think I shall ever vote for an old-line party again.

The
Liberals are no better.
Quite true. I think we can say that the same thing applies to the Liberal party.
That does not apply to some of us. Some of us predicted what would happen.
Are we planning now for that which may be a year, two years, three or four years ahead?

The
Liberals cannot see six months ahead, and here is the evidence.
I said I would not vote for an old-line party again. I did so once; I voted once upon a time for-believe it or not-the gentleman who is now Viscount Bennett.
Shame on you! You should have known better.

I will ask the hon. member for Bow River not to rub it in too hard.
Those are all the observations I wish to make. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe may rise in his place and say, "Let us not play politics"; but if politics is played at all, it is played on the grounds of political opportunism. Let us not be political opportunists; let us be in this whole matter as statesmanlike as we can.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
We are discussing the proposals of the Minister of Finance?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, as the Prime Minister intimated just before recess.

I listened with very great interest to the statement of the minister the other night in which he described the considerations which induced the government to proceed

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
by the particular method which it has adopted. As far as my observation goes, I would be inclined to think the country has received it, as a declaration of policy, with a good deal of acquiescence. But the minister realizes, as I think the public realizes, that the government has embarked upon an undertaking the working out of which, on the administrative side, will be accompanied by intense difficulty. The minister has not belittled the difficulties. I assume the committee will wish to discuss those difficulties as hon. members see them.
A difficulty which, it seems to me, will have to be met is that the retailer finds himself in this position. Following the accustomed method of trade, he has ordered ahead. In some instances he has had to order, months ahead, the commodities which he needs to maintain his stock. In those months the wholesaler's price to the retailer has in all probability risen. The retailer has his shelves somewhat full of those articles that he is accustomed to deal in, has probably not raised his prices; the prices which he has been charging the public relate to the costs at which he provided himself with those goods. But those prices ruling through the period of September and October will no longer recompense him for what he will have to pay for the goods ordered in the months preceding the period. I wonder whether the government have given consideration to that matter, and consider it as one which must be met, and whether the minister can describe any methods by which it may be met.
It appears to me that recognition must be given to that difficulty. If it is not given, as far as I can see, it just means that the retailer is left in the position of having to take that loss. If the retailer at large through this country, be he the small man or chain-store shareholder, has to pay more to the wholesaler for the goods he has ordered prior to this period, then he will have to absorb the loss. I do not know if the government is preparing to load that loss on to the retailer who appears to me to be alone in having to carry it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a problem peculiar to the retailer. It may apply to the wholesaler as well, or the processor. The problem is a very real one, and consideration has been given to various methods of meeting it. I am not in a position to say which of those methods or what method will be adopted. I should like to hear hon. members present the difficulties, and shall take note of their representations. But I think it would prejudice the whole working of the scheme if I were to indicate what the board may or may not do. I am not in a position to say that at the moment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does the minister not think that at the beginning at all events, no matter how much good-will there may be toward the aim which the government has in view-and I do not think anyone has disparaged1 that aim, at least I have not; I was criticizing the means by which it was to be achieved, not the end in view-does he not think that in a great experiment like this it w'ould be fair to say that the whole thing will be more or less a matter of trial and error until the weak spots are found and the holes are plugged?
I have in mind the case of a manufacturer who has to bring in parts, some from the United States, if he is allowed to do so, where he thinks he can buy them more cheaply than locally, even after paying the exchange and duty. The manufacturers are fearful that their costs will be increased but that their selling prices upon which they base their bids to their customers in the ordinary course of dealing will be frozen. They send their travellers out months in advance to take orders before the goods are made, for example boot and shoe manufacturers. On a rising market a manufacturer simply cannot sell at the prices at which he has been asked to, and he just has to cancel his order. I have found that case. I assume that in a case like that, if he makes the proper representation to the board and if the board are satisfied as to the bona fides of his position, they will grant him some relief. Is it to be a case of every man applying on his own behalf, or will they be heard in classes? These are thoughts that have been running through my mind. I do not see how any hard and fast principles can be laid down to govern a position like this.
While I am on my feet may I offer a suggestion to the minister, who rather deprecated the suggestion I made the other day that these prices had been frozen on an uneven level. That may not be true with regard to the whole commodity picture, but certainly it is true with regard to certain commodities. I think it is true with respect to agricultural commodities, other than wheat, because definitely this does not govern wheat. I think it is true with respect to agricultural production in my own province. That production is not as large as it might be, but that is the reaction I get from those in the business. Take, for example, those who raise potatoes, one of the most important productions we have in our province. The hon. member for V-ictoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) knows very much more about it than I do; and I know he holds that view very strongly.
I suggest to the minister that it must of necessity become more or less a matter of trial and error, and I am afraid that the man

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
who pushes most strongly, who pulls the hardest, who is capable intellectually and financially of making out the best case, will win out, while the little man, who perhaps cannot make himself heard, who has not the money to present his case, may suffer.
He always has.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have grave fears for the safety and the future of the small dealer in this country under this project. The big chain-store man or the big department store is in a better position to sustain any shock that may come. The little fellow who marks his goods, not on the basis of the cost of replacement but rather on the basis of the cost to him on the shelves, is going to take what will be to him a very severe licking. That is my fear, though I hope I may be wrong.
On the other hand, I believe that if the government wdshes to perform a national service, with which I think in principle we all agree-namely, to prevent inflation-we ought to ask for the whole-hearted support of everybody to see if this thing cannot be put over. That is my attitude at the moment; yet I do not see how it can be done by a central body here in Ottawa, in a far-flung country like Canada, where the little fellow cannot make himself heard. Perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite may be able to help the minister; I hope they can.

I should like to endorse the remarks of the two previous speakers. Unfortunately it is the man who has acted from the decent point of view who is going to suffer most. A retailer, confronted with a sharply advancing price, has two alternatives; I was a retailer during the last war and I know how it worked out. When he sees prices going up he can do what the better element perhaps would do, continue to sell at the old price until his stock is exhausted, and then raise his price; or he might say, as the leader of the opposition says, "Well, I will only regard the cost of replacement," and thus take advantage of the rising market, knowing that people can not buy the commodity for less from any other retailer. In that way he could secure a greater profit than ordinarily would be the case.
That is what has happened here. The man who said, "I will not increase my price beyond the basis of what I had to pay," is going to be stung. The man who increased his price because he saw the market rising will get off, because he raised his price during the control period. The result will be that the man who did the fair thing will be stuck, not only for the immediate future but apparently for a good long time, because whoever drew up these regulations appears not to have taken account of that lag, so to speak, between the wholesale and the retail price. Some retailers buy their stuff six months ahead; but whatever the period may be, there is a lag. The leader of the opposition spoke about the small man not making himself heard. I can tell the committee that the small man in my district is making himself heard, because since this thing was announced I have received nearly a hundred letters begging me to bring the matter to the attention of the minister or the house.
As I say, this is going to be a permanent thing; it will not be only one temporary loss, for the sake of the convenience of the departmental official; it will go on indefinitely, because the merchant will be compelled to sell at the price obtaining during the control period. But the price has been raised already by the wholesaler, and even if he is not permitted to increase it any more, it remains at that level. I have a letter in my office now in which a man mentions one brand of coffee. He says he is paying more for that coffee now than he was retailing it for during the four-week period. He anticipated having to increase the price as soon as his stock ran out, but unfortunately he did not increase his price during the period in question and now he is condemned to sell at the lower price for the duration of the war. On the other hand, the wholesaler will be able to sell the coffee at the price fixed during the latter part of the four-week period, which will create a gross injustice as far as the small man is concerned, as the leader of the opposition has said.
It seems to me it should not be very difficult to take care of that situation. Any adjustment would have to be made only once; then the wholesaler would not be permitted to increase his price again, and there would be no more trouble. In the case of almost every retailer there has been some increase in wholesale prices during that period, but unless an adjustment of this kind is made, the man who was decent about the thing will be the sufferer.

In saying a few words with regard to this matter I do not wish either the minister or the committee to take it that I am criticizing control in itself. I think we are all satisfied that under the circumstances controls of various kinds will have to be put into operation, and the only matter about which I am concerned is that .these controls should affect everyone as equally as possible. We are not going to put into operation controls which will impose

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
restrictions in any way without hurting somebody, but what I do wish to avoid is any grossly unequal distribution of the burden that will be caused.
In reply to the hon. member for Yale the minister suggested that the wholesaler was affected in much the same way as the retailer. To a certain extent that may be true, but I believe the minister will agree that, generally speaking, the wholesaler will be better able to carry the burden than the retailer. The man who will be concerned most of all is the retailer with a small business, because it will affect his living. There is only a very small margin between what is sufficient to keep him going and what will cause him to close up shop altogether.
The minister has made out a pretty good case; obviously he cannot say at the moment what his department will do in the matter, but if we could have an understanding that these questions will receive the utmost possible consideration, then I think we shall be satisfied. It may be said, I suppose, that many of the small retail businesses are uneconomical. I believe that is true; but until we find some method by which the people who are in these businesses, and who would be put out of business by the control, can make a livelihood in other occupations, great care should be taken to see that they are not unduly affected by the controls instituted, as has been outlined by the hon. member for Yale.

When the Minister of Munitions and Supply was introducing the subject matter which he reviewed in a previous speech, this matter was discussed with particular reference to raw materials required for war industries. That is a problem as far as his department is concerned; discussion appears at page 4241 of Hansard.
Now, on the invitation of the Minister of Finance, I direct the attention of the Minister of Finance to the same subject. A portion of the raw materials referred to is used in the manufacture of war materials, but a larger portion is used in the ordinary commerce of the country. In days gone by, the market for primary products was usually based on what could be obtained for the exportable surplus. Invariably, in common with agricultural products, they found the price which prevailed for the exportable surplus, especially if it were shipped to the United Kingdom, in view of the fact that, in days gone by, the United Kingdom had received their supplies from India and Europe, was considerably lower than the price on the domestic market in Canada.

To-day, either fortunately or unfortunately, the only export market of any value that we have is in the United States, and prices in that market are riding anywhere from 10 per cent to 60 or 70 per cent higher than the ceiling price in Canada.
I arrive at the ceiling price from this deduction.: through the years raw materials have been contracted for. As I said before, contracts were ordinarily made in the months of November and December for the twelve-month period following. The contract prices of December, 1940, provide the ceiling prices and the base period in this legislation. Meantime, due to industrial activity in the United States, the market in that country has risen considerably above the Canadian ceiling price.
I appreciate that the minister's problem is a very difficult one, and I am going to offer him one suggestion to which he might give some thought, and which I believe would help him with his problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is the hon. member talking
about rubber?

I am speaking
about hides, in particular-hide trimmings, and commodities of that kind. I refer not only to hides alone, but to split trimmings. I am afraid if I gave the minister the complete nomenclature of all primary products, he probably would not understand it all. Hides, however, constitute one commodity among a number of others.
For instance, murrain hides in Detroit are selling anywhere from two cents to six cents a pound higher than in Windsor. I know about the export situation in that connection. But in respect of by-products from split trimmings -that is, after the hides are split-a million pounds were shipped out of this country last year. The contract price in December, 1940, in the case of wet was $22 a ton, and dry, $30. The value to-day in Boston is $45 for wet and as high as $60 for dry. That is an example of the commodities I have in mind.
Of course this is not a commodity which will upset the whole economic set-up of Canada, but it is an illustration of many other commodities. The trading in this commodity amounts to probably only a thousand tons a year. But the suggestion I am going to put on record is that the minister should have access to the records of exporters of raw materials of this and other kinds to the United States for the preceding year. It may be that he would have the information for two or three years preceding. He would ascertain the names of those desirous of shipping products out of Canada, and bleeding this country of raw materials so necessary for the making

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
of war requirements. The minister's department could take a record of the individual shippers and, before issuing export licences, could have those shippers declare what they had shipped in years gone by. In that way he may be able to hold the situation in hand.
What will happen will be that shippers who have been loyal to Canadian industry by selling their products at home will be in the unhappy position of receiving a little less for their products, if they sell them for the ceiling price in Canada. On the other hand, those who through branch plants connections in the United States still ship to that country will get the advantage of a higher market. I therefore suggest that the minister's department see to it that shipments abnormally large compared with those in previous years are not allowed to leave Canada, and in that way avoid a scarcity of raw materials to keep Canadian industry supplied.
I know the minister's department has already received representations in that respect, because I was interviewed in Toronto by a Chicago concern which made representations concerning the export of beef hides and calf skins from Canada to the United States. That is one example. If his department takes a firm stand, I am sure he will get the cooperation of Canadian industry. I realize some of the difficulties, but I hope he will give consideration to the suggestion I make.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
How do these price control regulations affect the price of wheat? As I understand it. the ceiling price will be the average between September 15 and October 11, which was about 77-3 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was the highest price.
The highest in that period was about 77-3 cents. But the minimum price would still be in effect. The price would be allowed to fluctuate between 70 and 77-3 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is only for domestic sales, and does not apply to export sales.

I cannot help being amused at the apparent about-face on the part of the government in respect of certain matters in their financial policy. For instance, on various occasions between 1935 and 1939 we stressed the fact, when it was desirable to put certain projects into operation, that provided we had the necessary men and material to carry out those projects, it was quite a simple matter to arrange for the financing of them. In other words, we stressed the fact that anything physically possible and 14873-276
desirable could be made financially possible. We remember that whenever we suggested such a thing in the house we were ridiculed by the former Minister of Finance.
It is interesting to note that since the declaration of war the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) have stressed on various occasions that everything that in the physical sense can be done to win this war will be made financially possible. In other words, they are taking exactly the same stand as we took in peace time, but apparently they are not prepared to take that stand in peace time. They will take it only in war time.
Between 1935 and 1940 we stressed on many occasions that in order to develop our resources to their fidl capacity and maintain as high a standard of living as possible, it would be necessary to institute price control and, in certain instances, some degree of rationing. The present Minister of Finance took exception to that statement; in fact he took a very strong stand against any suggestion that we should introduce price control. May I read to the committee what he said on November 21, 1940, when the proposal was made by one of this group that we have price control. These are his words:
Price fixing of a few commodities, indeed rationing of a few commodities, is possible and need not have a very serious effect, but price fixing and rationing on a general scale have at least two disadvantages.
In the first place, this would call for bureaucratic interference in the private affairs of all Canadian citizens. Perhaps I am speaking a little bit figuratively here, but generally speaking there would have to be a government spy in every grocery store. The Germans did this with some success, but the Germans are experts as spies.
And then:
The whole habit of thought of the Canadian people, the dislike of intensive and general government intervention in their personal transactions and private affairs, would make a universal system of price fixing and rationing, even if it were practicable in Canada, far more odious, 1 am satisfied, than a system of taxation and borrowing out of savings, which is the policy of this government.
Every detail of our economic life would have to be controlled by someone sitting here in Ottawa.
It is true that the nazis in Germany have gone nearly as far as this with their price fixing and rationing. But even they, with a dictatorship and with years of experience before the war, have had to combine this price fixing with very heavy war taxation and with borrowing enormous sums at interest rates higher than we pay in Canada.
The minister made that statement as recently as November 21, 1940. According to

the minister, price control would necessitate placing a spy in every food store. If the minister is still of that opinion, I wonder whether he is starting to organize a gestapo and put spies in stores throughout the country. That is what he said in order to ridicule our proposal. I agree that his statement at that time was nonsense, but that is the language used by the Minister of Finance and the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Ralston) on almost every occasion when we made proposals to better the financial system. I agree that there is no reason of sense in that statement, that the minister went to extremes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said I did.

I am glad to hear the
minister admit that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not now, but I did then. I said that I was speaking figuratively, that that would bring about a system of regimentation, and so it will. We are going very far in that direction.

I am not criticizing the minister for introducing a form of price control. I think it is necessary, but the proposal made is a clumsy one. The minister would be well advised to adopt the price control proposal suggested by Major Douglas. That is what they have adopted to a certain extent in the United States with the stamp plan, and also in Great Britain with the system of compensated prices. I shall not deal with that now, but I may at another opportunity.
In his speech, the minister admitted that we in this group had always opposed inflation. I doubt if there is any group in this house more opposed to inflation. On the other hand, the minister stated that he was of opinion that our proposal would cause inflation. Let us go back to the years 1935 to 1939. We had half a million unemployed; industry was running in low gear; many plants were closed down or running at a small percentage of their capacity, and we had a favourable balance of payments in those years amounting to around 8200,000,000. In addition, there were a million people on relief. The ministers of the government were travelling all over the world in an effort to obtain foreign markets, but they were absolutely blind to the fact that in Canada there was a tremendous undeveloped market in the million people on relief and the many others who were having to accept a standard of living far below what was necessary.
Our proposal during that period was, first of all, that we should take steps to obtain effective control over the issue of currency

and credit. We realized that this wrould be necessary before we started any other financial reform. Then we contended that a certain proportion of the unemployed should be put to work on capital projects and a certain proportion in industries producing goods for consumption. The money paid out for capital projects would help to create an effective demand for the goods produced by the consumption goods industries. But we also stressed the fact that it was necessary to maintain a certain definite relationship between the production of capital goods and the production of consumer goods. We contended that capital production should be maintained at a sufficient volume so that the money paid out in its production would be at least equal to the deficiency which existed between the total price of consumer goods available for distribution and the effective demand against them.
I think we all know that from 1935 to 1939 our capital projects were down well below normal. On many occasions we advocated that these capital projects should be increased. We advocated slum clearance, road building, reforestation and many other projects. The money paid out to carry on these projects would have created an effective demand for consumer goods which could have been produced but which were not. Every time we made such a suggestion the Minister of Finance woidd ridicule it as being inflationary; at times he became almost hysterical.
We said that such a programme could be financed by the Bank of Canada, but we suggested that before the Bank of Canada was used for that purpose it was most necessary that we should obtain effective control over the issue of currency and credit. We had not that control at that time and we still have not that control. We suggested also that it would be necessary to institute a system of price control. I defy the minister to say that such a proposal as that could possibly cause inflation. The effect of carrying out that suggestion would have been to maintain production at its maximum level, or at least at a level sufficiently high to maintain a decent standard of living in this country. It was not inflation; it was simply stabilizing supply and demand.
We realize too well that since the declaration of war the situation has changed entirely. To-day we have a great expansion in the production of capital goods and the money paid out in this production is causing an increased demand for consumer goods. There is no longer a proper relationship between

The War-Finance-Piice Ceiling
the production of consumer goods and the production of capital goods. As the war goes on and we find it necessary to make a greater effort, we shall have to increase the production of capital goods. When we have exhausted our supply of labour it will become necessary to decrease the supply of consumer goods. We realize that it is absolutely necessary to have this relationship in war time.
The Minister of Finance says that this excess purchasing power should be drained off by a system of taxation and the sale of bonds. We agree that the people should be allowed to invest a certain amount of their money in savings certificates, to put aside a little for a rainy day, but we cannot understand why the people of this country should be forced into debt in order that certain people may have an investment, or, in other words, that we should curtail spending. We have always attacked the sale of bonds as being a dishonest and unsound system. We claim that it is	dishonest	because	it	is nothingmore or less than a misappropriation of the funds of future generations. We maintain that it is	unsound	because	we	shall bebuilding up a debt that can never be paid under the	orthodox	system	of	finance. Ihasten to add that when we say that we do not mean-the minister sometimes jumps to conclusions-that the people who are buying bonds to-day are not going to be paid. Of course they will be paid, but in paying those people the government will not be reducing the debt;	they will do it	by	refunding,
just as it has been done in the past.
The minister has stated that the ideal method of selling bonds would be to distribute them as evenly as possible throughout the nation. If we could make this a one hundred per cent distribution, if everyone held an equal amount of bonds, then everyone would be taxed to pay his own interest. We would all be taking in each other's washing and we would be no further ahead. The same thing could be accomplished by taxation. But this is not the situation; we know very well that a large percentage of the bonds are held by a small number of people. I know that the figures issued by the minister show a wide distribution, but that does not alter the fact that a large proportion of the bonds are held by a comparatively small number of people. We shall be taxing all the people to pay the majority of the interest due to a small number of the people, and that is not a desirable state of affairs.
As I say, we shall never be able to pay back this debt. That must be quite obvious. If the people to-day are not able to pay for
current production, then the people of the future will certainly not be able to pay for the goods they consume at that time as well as the goods we are using to-day but not paying for. If we adopted a real pay-as-you-go system, we would be paying for these goods as we used them and not be calling upon generations of the yet unborn to pay for the cost of this war. Some people will argue that we are fighting for democracy and therefore we have the right to expect the people of the future to help pay the cost. That argument has been used in connection with every war fought in the past. We are still paying for wars fought one hundred years ago. Every time we have another war our debt mounts and the problem becomes greater. The same thing will happen in the future. The people of that day will be asked to pay for this war. But I suggest that the people of the future will have sufficient troubles of their own without being asked to pay for the war we are fighting to-day.
The minister likes to hope that the tremendous revenues we are obtaining to-day will continue after the war. Why is it that we have such large revenues to-day? What is the main reason? I put forward two main reasons. In the first place we had monetary expansion to provide for maximum employment and increase the production of industry. Second, and perhaps more important, the government has become the largest purchaser of labour and commodities in the country. Is the government prepared to continue that policy after the war? If it is-and mind you, it is a complete change from the policy of the past-there is no reason why we cannot have in Canada after the war the greatest era of prosperity which the world has ever seen, because all the productive capacity for war purposes to-day will be available after the war to satisfy the needs of the people. But if we are going to be told, as we have been told already, that we shall have to tighten our belts to pay for the war, that all government projects will be curtailed and that there will be a general contraction of credit, then undoubtedly we are going to have in this country the greatest depression we have ever seen. I recall what was said of the last depression. Mr. Spinney, general manager of the Bank of Montreal, said that the main reason for the last depression was the great debt which had been incurred in the last war. Then I ask the Minister of Finance, if a two billion dollar debt for the last war caused a ten-year depression, what will the war debt at the end of this war cause? There is no question in my mind that we are headed for one of the worst depressions we have seen in

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
this country unless the government is prepared to depart from its former orthodox financing.
There is one other question to which I wish to refer. In the past in this house we have urged and we are still urging that to the extent that taxation and the sale of interest-free certificates will not provide the necessary revenue for the government, the services of the Bank of Canada should be used. It is interesting to note that many prominent bankers and economists are showing a complete change of mind on this subject, especially as regards the sale of bonds. If anybody went out during the last victory loan campaign and suggested that the sale of bonds was not the correct method of financing the war, his patriotism was likely to be called in question and he was likely to get a visit from the police the next day. As a matter of fact the police did visit people who criticized that method of financing the war. I have criticized it inside and outside this house both in peace time and in war time because it is a racket which becomes more contemptible in time of war. Let me quote what has been said in this regard by two authorities whose word cannot lightly be set aside: first, Lord Kindersley, who I understand is chairman of the National War Savings Committee in England and a director of the Bank of England. He is quoted in the April 9 issue of the Parliamentary Debates of the British House of Commons by Mr. Stokes, M.P., as having said:
I do not disagree with the expressed belief that it does not make a pennyworth of difference whether you subscribe or not, provided you bank your money and do not spend it.
The minister would agree with that statement because he has stated that the purpose of the sale of bonds and of taxation is primarily to curtail purchasing power. But if people are prepared to stop spending and to put their money in a bank, the same end is achieved, so far as not spending it is concerned, as if they had bought war savings certificates or bonds. The minister has stated in the house that the main purpose of taxation and the sale of bonds is not the raising of revenue but to curtail the spending of the people. That statement was also made by Professor Plumptre.
I want to quote one other authority in this regard. He goes a bit further than Lord Kindersley. I quote from the Western Producer of October 9, 1941, which has an editorial on the August letter of the Royal Bank of Canada. The editorial says in part:

Tlie same issue of the Royal bank letter went on to quote with apparent approval criticism voiced by the London Economist. That leading periodical is cited as having said:
"The whole cast of savings propaganda needs to be quite radically altered. The individual should be told that his duty is to reduce his consumption by every possible means. He should have the lesson driven home to him on every hoarding that every act of consumption uses shipping space and labour-the two scarcest of commodities. Once he has economized as much as he can, it matters very little what happens to the money he saves thereby-"
I drawr the attention of the Minister of Finance especially to this:
"The saving once done, it is of no advantage to the state to pile up enormous figures of subscriptions to savings certificates and war loan. Indeed it is to the state's advantage not to borrow' at two and a half per cent or three per cent if it can raise the money more cheaply, and the truly patriotic citizen is he who, having reduced his consumption to the absolute minimum, leaves his spare money in the bank."
I quite agree with that statement, and I think everybody should agree that it is far more patriotic to curtail your spending and not impose a debt on the nation than to curtail your spending through a process of increasing the national debt.
The minister is introducing a form of price control. It is a blanket price control. As I have stated, we believe that a better system could be introduced; nevertheless this plan will have the effect of preventing the exploitation of the people by certain industries. At the present time we have not effective control of the issue of currency and credit. Therefore I would ask the minister this question: Why does the government not take the necessary steps to obtain absolute and effective control of the issue of currency and credit and then, instead of obtaining credit through the chartered banks or financing the war by the issue of bonds, why not use the services of the Bank of Canada? Or perhaps I should ask this question rather: Is the government intending to utilize the services of the Bank of Canada? The minister in his speech left that question up in the air. He stated that he needed $600,000,000 but did not know where he was going to get it. He thought he had pushed taxation as far as he could and he did not like issuing any more bonds. He did not state what action the government proposed to take. I wonder whether he could at this time tell us what is the government's objection to utilizing the services of the Bank of Canada, having first of all obtained effective control of the chartered banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is one of those academic discussions which the hon. gentleman is very fond of starting in this house. I have engaged

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
in them before, but I really do not know that much advantage would be gained by entering upon another one to-night. If we are to do that, I will make some preparation, as the hon. gentleman has done, and then come back and we will have a debate of that kind if he wants it. But I do not see what is to be gained by it. He has his views as to how this war should be financed and we have our views. We have both put our respective views before the house and the country. He talks about the 8600,000,000 that I was speaking of the other night. I do not admit that that particular $600,000,000 is ever going to be needed, because that was the additional amount which would be needed after the price level rose by 20 or 30 per cent, and we do not intend that the price level shall rise.
With regard to whether we intend to borrow from the Bank of Canada, there has been some small borrowing, as the hon. gentleman knows, from the Bank of Canada. The returns which have been produced in the house have set out the borrowings from the chartered banks, from the public, and from the Bank of Canada. When the hon. gentleman asks me whether it is the intention of the government to borrow from the Bank of Canada, and how much we intend to borrow from the Bank of Canada, those are questions which I should not, and indeed cannot, answer at the present time.

Would the minister care to comment upon the August letter of the Royal Bank of Canada? I ask that question because throughout the country there is a great deal of discontent at the way in which the government is financing this war. There is a feeling that we are building up a debt which is going to have the effect of causing depression and a great deal of grief after the war. The statement in the Economist is a very clear one. It is one for which people in this country have been branded as unpatriotic when they make it. I do not think that stigma can be attached to the Economist, whose statement is quoted with apparent approval by the Royal bank. If it is a correct statement of fact, unquestionably something is wrong with the government's policy.	y.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To what statement is the hon. gentleman referring?
The one which I quoted from the Economist.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What part of it?
The one which stated that people would be just as patriotic or more patriotic if they placed their money in the banks rather than purchase bonds or war savings certificates with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whatever the validity of the statement may be, the fact is that if the money is not borrowed from persons, they do not place it in the banks, they spend it, and that exerts an upward pressure on the price level. Therefore, from a practical point of view the only thing to do is to secure the money from the people, to channel money back to the government from the people either by taxation or by borrowing. We cannot go very much further by taxation, so we have to do it by borrowing. We have to offer some incentive to people to lend money to the government; that is why we pay interest.
In other words, the government feels obliged to place the nation in debt rather than allow the people to spend the money. Surely the logical thing would be to increase taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The nation is in debt to itself.

That would be true only if everybody were buying an equal amount of bonds. I know we are assured by Mr. Towers that the greater the debt, the greater the prosperity: "Look at central Africa-no debt, no prosperity!" But that would be true only if everybody were buying an equal quantity of bonds. We know that is not the situation. We know the situation is that a very small percentage of the people hold by far the greater part of the bonds, so that for evermore the people of this country are going to be compelled to pay tribute to that small number of bondholders. That is why I contend that the correct procedure would be to tax those people rather than sell bonds to them. After all, the minister has stressed again and again that we should have a pay-as-you-go policy. When we take into consideration the tremendous sacrifices which are being made to-day in Europe and by our own people; when we call to mind that many are going as far as to give their lives, is it too much to expect that people in this country should be content to maintain their pre-war savings entire, and to have a fairly decent standard of living for the duration of the war, but that after the war they should not be any better off than they were at the start? The person who finds himself in that position should regard himself as exceedingly lucky. No one should expect to build up, as a result of this war, great accumulations of bonds which will largely represent profits from the war. It seems to me a very unfortunate state of affairs that when certain people buy, say half a million dollars worth of bonds, we call them patriots-patriots for having invested their money at three per cent in a gilt-edged security. I do not like the use of the word "patriot" to describe a man who, as a result of good business, is able to get hold of a

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
security which will provide him with three per cent for the rest of his life. We use the same word to honour the man who goes overseas and sacrifices his life. I should say that the correct procedure is. to tax those who have the greatest amount to lose as a result of this war; they should be prepared to make such sacrifices in line with the sacrifices which are being made overseas.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are less.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, no. On an analysis of about 320 companies which was made by the Bank of Canada, and which did not include certain classes of companies such as railways and some others, but covered 320 representative industries in Canada, it appeared that the profits after taxation had increased by 6 per cent in 1940 over 1930-which was a very moderate increase. The Financial Post made an analysis of the balance sheet of, I believe, 280 representative companies, and the conclusion to which they came was that the profits after taxation had increased 2-2 per cent. The increase in income after taxation has not been to any extent to commercial, industrial or financial corporations; it has been in the lower income earning groups. It is very largely in the wage-earning groups that the great increase has taken place in the incomes of the people of the Dominion of Canada. Of course, we tax them, but at a so much lower rate that their net incomes after taxation have been very substantially increased.

I should just like to
mention that I notice, from the returns of the profits of the chartered banks, that in the case of the Bank of Toronto the profit increased in 1940 from, I believe 16 per cent to 24 per cent after the taxation had been paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether that was after taxation or before, but I think it was before.
It stated "after taxation".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not sure about that. But that was 24 per cent upon the original capital, without rest, without reserves being taken into account; and as rest was not taken into account at all, it is open to question whether that is a fair basis. If a financial institution has been operating over a long period and has made profits in previous 3'ears and has a large rest fund, then, to take the earnings upon original capital, which may have been invested fifty years ago, is not a very sound test as to the earnings of the money actually employed in the business.

This price ceiling order in council is a great experiment, and, as has been said, will be a matter of trial and error, but I think the minister should have the cooperation of the general public in working it out. At page 4156 of Hansard the minister is reported as saying:
