I have here an article from the Toronto Globe and Mail of Tuesday the 11th instant, quoting the Searle index. It says:
Searle Grain Company makes the following points:
United States government has adopted the principle of 1913-14 parity, which means that agricultural products should have the same purchasing power now over the things that farmers have to buy as they had in 1913-14.
For wheat in the United States to be at the 1913-14 parity would require a price of approximately $1.22 in store Chicago. To-day May wheat, Chicago, is actually $1.19 a bushel.
For Canadian wheat to be at 1913-14 parity would similarly require a price of about $1.20 for No. 1 northern in store Fort William. To-day No. 1 northern in Fort William is 72| cents a bushel.
A maximum of 223 million bushels has been set for the amount of wheat that western farmers are permitted to deliver during this present crop year.
In order to narrow somewhat the wide gap that exists between the farmers' low income from wheat and the high cost of the things that farmers have to buy, the government has given wheat growers certain bonuses which we estimate amount to 52 million dollars. (An additional 8 million dollars to farmers who grow grain other than wheat.)
Including these government bonuses the total income from wheat during this present crop year will amount to about 152 million dollars as compared with 234 million dollars revenue from wdieat last year, and 441 million dollars in 1928.
This is that original basis .of which we spoke.
Certainly I think the great mass of the agricultural population must receive some further consideration to put them on a basis of equality with organized labour and industry, and while, as I stated, I think the minister should have the cooperation of all the people of the country, certainly this will have to be equalized in some manner.

It is one of the disadvantages of the system we have adopted in this committee that it is the right and privilege of every one of us to talk, as regards the particular minister whose policies are under debate, on any phase of his activities. The result is that twenty men all want to talk about different subjects, and it produces an awful lack of coherence. If the chairman had authority, once a subject is introduced, to have it threshed out and then, so to speak, pass that item, we would get along much better.
We started this evening, when there were not very many hon. members present, with a. statement from the minister that he would like to hear hon. members state their views on the question of a condition which compels retailers to sell at a price lower than they
are paying wholesale now, because that is what it amounts to. The minister invited expressions of opinion, but only three hon. members have spoken on that. Going back to that feature for a moment, I think the minister indicated that when he heard our views he would take them into consideration. It seems such a simple matter that for the good of the project which we all hope will be a success, namely this price restriction policy, it would almost seem impossible to have it said that a very considerable body of people are compelled to sell goods for less than what they pay for them and carry their overhead as well, which generally runs to from fifteen to twenty-five per cent. It is obvious that this is not desirable. Suppose we carry it far enough and put them out of business. Some people have the same regard for retailers as hon. members in the far corner have for banks; they think they are very bad, but we cannot do without them, and to put them out of business would be a disadvantage.
An. hon. MEMBER:	They serve a useful
purpose.

They serve a useful purpose.
It will hurt the success of the scheme if it is demonstrated that, a certain class of people are compelled to sell for less than they pay, and these men who have written to me show, without any trouble, that to be the situation.
While I have the floor I wish to put another situation before the minister. I do not quite know how he comes to have control of this matter, but in these days one is liable to find any department under any minister. I rang up a department yesterday and asked the young lady what minister a certain branch came under, and she courteously said she did not know but she would find out. Half an hour later she told me it was under a totally different minister from the one I anticipated- which information I afterwards found to be wrong.
The minister has become heir in some way to the war-time prices and trade board, which board is responsible for the prohibition of the export from British Columbia of dogfish and soupfin sharks' livers. It has been the subject of a brief presented by the fishermen; no doubt he has seen it. To put it as shortly as possible, the board have put a prohibition on the export of these livers to the United States market. Apparently the custom was, in the early part of the war, to send them to the United States to be processed, on the understanding that the product would find its way to Britain where it is badly needed; it is a valuable source of vitamins. There was possibly some idea that

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
this was not being done, that it was being retained in the United States, where they also have a shortage. At any rate the board put on an embargo.
The result from the fisherman's point of view is this. The price being paid by United States buyers to United States fishermen for dogfish livers is about 44 cents a pound, and for the soupfin sharks' livers, about S8 a pound, while the price to the Canadian fishermen for dogfish livers is about 11 cents a pound in the Vancouver area and for soupfin sharks' livers, between $2 and $3 a pound. They say the board has informed them that the embargo is temporary and may be lifted in the future. The result will be that the dealers who have been buying these commodities in British Columbia will make an enormous profit, and the fishermen will be out the difference between 11 and 44 cents. They suggest one or two remedies: either lift the embargo, or allow clearance for Canadian vessels so that they can fish in the same areas and take the catch to the United States, or that the government should buy this stuff at United States market prices.
It does appear to be one of those cases which call for recognition of the fact that when a man has produced or caught or grown something, he should be permitted to market it to the best advantage. The difference in price is due entirely to this embargo; in other words, our fishermen are suffering as a consequence of this step having been taken. It may be argued that it is necessary to retain this in Canada so that it may find its way to Britain; but we have only two small plants in British Columbia handling this article, one in Prince Rupert and, I think, two in Vancouver; they are processing it only to what might be called a minor extent, I believe ultimately it has to be sent east before the process can be completed.
These fishermen have made out a good case from their point of view. They say it is not fair that they should be the goats to such an enormous extent. Of course we know this is war time and we must protect ourselves and the British nation; but the idea seems to be that it is going to Britain anyway, that the embargo is going to be lifted shortly, and in the meantime these men who have been buying it up in British Columbia will reap an enormous profit. Therefore I should like the minister at least to promise to look into the matter, which is rather complicated. If he will study the brief he will see the argument they have put forward. This seems to be a fairly genuine case, and I believe the fishermen are entitled to the very best price the market will provide.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I read over the brief last night, and I have sent for some information with regard to it. There are some things about the brief which I do not understand, and in order to understand it I require some information from the war-time prices and trade board, which I have not received as yet. I will look into the situation.

For a few moments I should like to refer to one or two features of the public policy of the Minister of Finance which have developed since the house met last June. Last night St. Paul's hall in Yorkville, where Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, a former finance minister, used to speak, was destroyed by fire. It was in the Prime Minister's old constituency of York East, and where he used the phrase, "I had to sleep on the strong-box." It seems to me that since the war started, many of the old policies of the Liberal party have been gradually discarded in favour of national socialism. We had a victory loan not long ago, with a great flourish of trumpets and the usual posters, billboards, full-page advertisements, military parades, bands and so on, which, according to a return brought down by the minister, yielded almost $900,000,000. It cost eight and a quarter million to put over. In that return, however, the minister forgot to include the cost of the troops, a huge sum all over Canada, who were used for publicity stunts at a time when they should have been training for active service. They are used also from time to time in the war savings certificates campaign, and I protest against that sort of thing.
There is no coordination between the various government departments. The minister is taking twice as much money as he should take from the pockets of the people in these victory loans, and in maintenance charges, in income tax and all the rest of it. I believe the victory loan cost the government too much, and at the same time I believe the rate of interest is not what it should be.
When parliament adjourned last June the government said they would take up with the government at Washington the possibility of applying lease-lend act to the understanding reached at Ogdensburg as it applied to Canada. They also said that during the adjournment an attempt would be made to see if the exchange regulations could not be eased a little, particularly with regard to amounts not exceeding S100, for the tourist trade. Now, after nearly four months, we find that nothing at all has been done to

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
ease exchange or to allow Canada to come under the lease-lend act for part of its work of home defence.
I have charged that the minister is taking too much money out of the pockets of the taxpayers. Almost 45 per cent of the money he is spending on home defence could and should come under the lease-lend act, because [DOT]hat money is being spent to protect Canada's neutrality in case the United States is attacked by a foreign power, and is for America's defence. That is the basis of our whole defence policy. No effort has been made, apparently, to point out to the government of the United States that Canada is spending these huge sums of money on what is called home defence. Actually there is no such thing as home defence; it will not amount to a snap of one's fingers in defeating Hitler. We spend all that money jointly to aid America as part of its first line of defence were she attacked.
As I pointed out last June when discussing this department of the government, there is no coordination between the various departments. They seem to be able to spend as much money as they like and spend money like water. Where is the auditor general with his vast power? Every department has its own auditors. The auditor general is not fulfilling his functions under the Audit Act. What is the matter with the treasury board that it allows these huge expenditures"? Not long ago we had the Minister of Agriculture announcing a policy which will cost the country over $100,000.000, and which is to be brought into operation by order in council. That money has to be found somewhere, and a large part of it will come from the income tax. The small taxpayer, who has to pay real estate taxes, interest on mortgages, insurance, and all that sort of thing, simply is not able to carry the load because he is taxed to death. Now that the government is taking so much more out of his pocket, with his fixed income he finds it almost impossible to carry on. I had hoped that during the adjournment the minister might work out with the treasury board some way of eliminating a great many of these expenditures, because, when all is said and done, a great deal of the money the minister is collecting for home defence will never be used to defeat the enemy. It seems that the various departments do not have to apply to the minister when they want to spend money. They simply say they are going to spend it, and it is spent. The Minister of Munitions and Supply goes ahead with a policy costing millions of dollars. He does not know how it is going to be financed and neither does anyone else. Then we have the Department of National War Services, which never should 14873-277
have been created, which does its work in a very roundabout way, duplicating the defence departments.
My principal point is that all the departments spending money should be brought under the control of the Minister of Finance and the auditor general. In the olden days that was the situation. I have referred to one minister of finance, Hon. Alexander Mackenzie. In the old days there was some control; we had an auditor general, Mr. McDougall, who checked up on all these expenditures before a dollar was released by the finance department. There should be some central authority for all these commitments. In England it took nearly two hundred years of civil war before parliament obtained control over expenditures in peace and war alike. Now we are losing that control; we are here to-day and away tomorrow, and in the recess every minister just goes to work and spends money like water. Not by the widest stretch of the imagination could some of these expenditures be said to be for war purposes. As I have pointed out already, they are very largely for home defence, and home defence will never win this war.
In conclusion I should like to mention a matter which the minister promised to look into during the recess, because it reacts severely on soldiers and civilians alike. I refer to the question of a national moratorium on mortgages for soldiers and civilians. When I brought up the question last week, the minister replied that it was a matter of policy. I think it is about time he came down out of the clouds and obtained some control over these shark loan companies, some of which charge soldiers and others 200 per cent interest, as well as over the departments of this government that are spending so much of the money of the taxpayers.
I believe the greater part by far of the Conservative vote of this country comes from the working classes, who are paying a great share of the taxes being collected by the minister. I am one of those Conservatives who do not believe in the nationalization of our industries or of the means of production. Neither do I believe in collectivization or many of these other social doctrines which have been taken up by the Liberal party and have been expressed by the government since we met last June. It will lead eventually to the abolition of all private property once the government, through its many boards, abolish all private enterprise and thrift and retail and wholesale business with all these artificial barriers and burdens. I do not believe, once the government, through its boards and officials, control everything, we

Under this policy of nationalization everybody will be working for the government, the land owner will disappear and the farmer become a paid official, if the programme is carried out to its logical conclusion. It would seem that the government hope by taxation so to discourage the owners of land that they will be willing to abandon their properties on any terms. As a member of the opposition I object to the fact that this vast life and death contest, this great war we are in, is being used as a means for bringing state socialism on a huge scale to Canada. I wonder why the opposition fall for it, and why they do not raise more objection to the inequality of it. Thrift, and the hereditary principles upon which this country has become great will have passed away, while this is taking place. I should hope that in the recess of parliament the Minister of Finance would assert his rights and prerogatives, and see to it that there is some coordination and central check in respect of these expenditures, and so reduce his budgets with a large share to capital and not so much to income.

Not only have we the boards I have indicated, but we have a joint defence board. It is binding Canada for the next hundred years, and doing it over the head of this parliament. Things are being done by it to which agreement has never been given by the House of Commons.
What is this lease-lend act? It is just what the chairman of the United States Senate has said. It is lease and lend, and he quoted Mr. Coolidge that they are simply hiring out money to Canada, for what? Canada is financing munitions for England1. There will be a day of reckoning, and they will make a demand on Canada for payment under the lease-lend act. It will be pointed out that there must be so much from Canada for this war. They will not be satisfied in Washington with payment by old, obsolete ships, but will want gold, because the United States have nearly all the gold in the world.
This opposition is not doing its duty unless it asserts the Conservative principle of conducting this war on a proper basis. It may be necessary to do some price fixing, and if properly administered that would do no harm. But it should be done only to a limited extent, and certainly not to the extent to which the minister has gone.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few observations I intend to make respecting the matter of the ceiling on prices. I believe we all agree that the minister made a most able presentation when he placed before the house and country the order in council. It constitutes the greatest single act of regimentation that has ever been introduced in this country. Similar action has become necessary in various parts of the world. A similar type of legislation was introduced in Australia on October 8, 1939, freezing the prices as at August 31 of that year. While the principle is that of controlling the operation of the economic laws, nevertheless it has worked out in that country with a reasonable degree of success.
The information I have with regard to Australia shows that in consequence of price fixing in that country, the increase in prices of foods and groceries from the outbreak of the war until October 1, 1941, was about 3 per cent compared with an increase of over 40 per cent in the same period of the last war. For the cost of living as a whole, including rent, clothing and miscellaneous items, the increase since the outbreak of this war has been 8-6 per cent compared with over 30 per cent in the corresponding period of the last war, and wholesale prices in this

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
war have increased by approximately 15 per cent compared with over 50 per cent in the same period of the last war.
As far as the principle is concerned, I think one and all are agreed that in the interests of preventing inflation some such legislation should be introduced. But I do not agree with the minister when he contends that the proper way in which to introduce it is by order in council. He says it would have been dangerous to have the date fixed by parliament, on account of the probability of evasion being practised. To guard against such a possibility, an order in council could have been passed fixing the date when the legislation would go' into effect, before the legislation was brought before parliament. Then parliament would have been in a position, with legislation before it, for the members to discuss each and every clause, each and every section, and, through debate, suggest necessary changes.
It is hard to conceive the reason the government had in calling parliament together when only two days before the opening of parliament, through an order in council the most drastic regimentation ever applied in Canada was brought into being. Was parliament not to be trusted? Could parliament not be trusted to debate the matter, point by point, if the legislation was introduced in the ordinary way?	The minister says, "Well, the
government could not tell just how long parliament would argue." The date fixed, namely, November 17 as the original date for the application of the order in council, and now postponed to December 1, was far enough in advance to have permitted full debate.
If this matter had been brought before parliament, there would have been a real justification for the calling of this session. We could have considered such a measure item by item. I remember well that last spring when the Minister of Agriculture introduced his order in council with respect to summer-fallowing he introduced the regulations one day, and amended them before the print was quite dry. Then a new set of regulations was presented; then he added a further amended set, and finally issued a revised edition, all because the terms had not been clarified by debate. Why did the government not place this matter before parliament and give the members of the house an opportunity to discuss the several items clause by clause? I should like now to refer to one particular clause which I think is most dangerous. Section 8 reads:
Nothing contained in these regulations shall be deemed to supersede any provision of any order heretofore made by the board or to 14873-277}
derogate from any power conferred on the board by the war-time prices and trade regulations and-
This is what I object to:
-without restricting the generality of this provision, the board, in its discretion, may vary any maximum price, may prescribe other or additional terms or conditions of sale, may exempt any person or any goods or services or any transaction wholly or partly from the provisions of these regulations.
That is a terrific power to place in the hands of any board, giving it the power to discriminate between individuals.

Mr. Chairman, from various ministers we had a comprehensive review of the activities of the government. Some of the government's accomplishments have been very satisfactory while others have not been so impressive, at
least to some of us. From the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) we have had figures of the production of small arms and explosives that were very good, but this war is not likely to be won by small arms but rather with tanks, aeroplanes, ships and heavy ordnance, but as yet, after twenty-seven months of war, our production of these arms is not so satisfactory.
It seems to me that the government should have cut out civilian spending at a much earlier date than they did. According to the bureau of statistics, in the month of September, 1941, we were spending one million dollars more on cars and trucks for civilian use in Canada than we did in the corresponding month in 1940. Yet the minister of munitions admits that we are in need of the steel for use in our shipyards. It seems to many of us that the government is following very much the same policy as it did in peace time; that is, doing nothing until forced to it by pressure of public opinion.
Public opinion in Canada to-day with regard to our war effort is much ahead of the government. I believe that the great majority of our people are prepared to see complete mobilization of our whole wealth and resources, both material and human, for an all-out war effort, and the government has had various representations made to it to that effect by various organizations across the country. The Canadian Legion made one of the most comprehensive recommendations yet made to the government, and I personally believe that it is one which the government would do well to follow. It seems to me that in Canada to-day, instead of having an all-out war effort we are still using the wasteful methods of the voluntary approach. We are spending on advertising and salesmanship, for instance, money which could be much better spent on war materials. In eveiy paper we see pages of advertising trying to sell the people of Canada luxury goods. On other pages will be seen advertising by the government asking people not to spend money on luxuries. On yet another page will be seen an advertisement by the Department of National War Services urging the people to save the very paper in which we are contradicting ourselves. These things seem very contradictory to the man on the street. Surely we cannot call that an all-out war effort?
During the summer I have heard many expressions like this while travelling through Saskatchewan: "Why should I buy war savings certificates and save gas? The government will only use the money to hire another inspector and buy him gas to drive round." That is not the spirit that is going to win this war.

I think remarks like that were made largely by reason of the appointment of great numbers of inspectors under the acreage bonus scheme. During the last sitting of the house the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), when he introduced this scheme, told us that they would probably use the inspectors they had working under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, approximately one hundred, and it might be necessary, he said, to hire an additional twenty-five inspectors. As a matter of fact, however, we have inspectors for every municipality in Saskatchewan, and there are over three hundred, and inspectors I believe for every local improvement district in the province. That applies, I believe, also to Alberta and Manitoba.
When this government have demonstrated by definite action that they are prepared to mobilize the wealth and resources and manufacturing capacity of Canada for an all-out war effort without profit to anyone, they need have no fear about the mobilization of the human resources of this country. If we are to have an all-out war effort, which is the objective of all members of this house, we must have in Canada much greater equality of sacrifice than we have at the present time. This year we floated in Canada one of the largest war loans in our history. Before launching the campaign the Minister of Finance did what I think was a wise thing. He called together some of the best financial experts in the country and business men with a nation-wide reputation, and they laid down plans for the campaign. They allotted quotas for the various provinces. The quota for Saskatchewan was, I believe, some $8,000,000, and for Ontario some 8300,000,000. The population of Saskatchewan was between 900,000 and 1,000,000 and the population of Ontario about 3,000.000. These people realize where the wealth of this country lies. As a matter of fact, there were several companies in this country, I believe, each of which was able to subscribe more to our war loan than the quota allotted to a million people in Saskatchewan.

Mr. ILSLEY": I did not say, because I do not knowr that. I would be astonished if they had. Some may have been sold, not very much, I think.

It still remains a fact that these people realized that Saskatchewan, containing a million people, could afford to raise only $8,000,000 because in that province we are engaged largely in agriculture, and agriculture during the last ten years has been the most poorly paid industry in this country. The leader of the opposition stated that it was the insurance companies which were taking out the most of these loans. As a matter of fact, I saw a report in the paper yesterday that the profits in the first nine months of this year of the International Nickel company were $25,000,000, and they had listed among their assets some $32,000,000 of treasury bills and securities. That is more than is held, I believe, by the million people in Saskatchewan. I cannot agree that there is any equality of sacrifice in this country while these conditions prevail. I believe that if, at the beginning of this war, the government had taken over every resource in Canada and had then called in the best brains of this country to plan intelligently their very best use, without regard to any private interest or advantage to any section or class in this country, we would have had a very much more effective war effort.
It seems to many of us that the war effort has been held up by the refusal of industry, in many instances, to expand their plants beyond a capacity which they believe could be economically used in peace time. After unnecessary delay, the government have had to provide the capital for the additional expansion which they require. Industry has been given charge of the building and the operation of it, and, upon the minister's own statement, has received the assurance that the use of this additional plant and equipment will be abandoned by the government after the war is ov.er. It seems to me that if the government wish to raise money in this country to build these plants and their equipment, one of the best methods they could use would be to assure the people that when the war is over, this additional plant and equipment which the people have built and paid for will be used to produce the goods which at the present time we are being asked to do without. We

The fact is therefore, that agriculture to-day in practically every part of Canada is in a serious position, and in western Canada in a desperate position. The income of the grain growers has been drastically reduced. I know the Minister of Agriculture may produce figures to show that this situation is perhaps not as serious as some of us represent it to be. It may not be to the minister, who has a salary to live on as well as his farm, but I know the people of Saskatchewan, I know the conditions under which they are living, and I know those conditions are serious.
I should like, in proof of that statement, to give some cases which have come to my attention during the year. May I say that my constituency is one of the best in Saskatchewan, one in which we have never had a crop failure, have always had good crops, and in which a considerable part of our income is derived from dairy products and live stock, not all grain. This summer I went into one of the districts in which people from the ' 
southern part of the province have been reestablished. I went to the chairman of the school board and questioned him regarding the school in that district. He told me they had built a new school there the year before. He showed me the register. That register showed that there were seventy-five children of school age in the district. They built the little schoolhouse themselves out of logs and made their own desks and blackboard. I asked him how many children were attending, and he told me that during the summer months they had an average attendance of about fifty, but during the winter the attendance had dropped to twenty-five. I asked why. Well, he said, the clothing allowance to the people of that district during the last winter had been $5 a head, a family of seven receiving an allowance of $35 on which to clothe the family for the year. Because of that the children could not attend school; the parents could afford to dress only a few of the brighter ones and send them. I asked what salary they were paying the teacher. He said that his own daughter was doing the teaching, that they had promised her $700 a year, the minimum set by the Saskatchewan government, but they had been able to pay her only $350 and had given her a note for the rest. To-day that school is closed, and in the constituency which I represent there are from three hundred to five hundred children who will not be able to attend school this winter owing to lack of clothing or because the school is closed by reason of its being impossible to pay the teacher's salary. The secretary of the teachers' federation in Saskatchewan made the statement that he believes that during this winter there will be probably two hundred such schools closed in Saskatchewan simply because the agricultural income in that province is not sufficient to maintain the educational facilities we should have.
Another instance I should like to relate has to do with the question of medical attention. In many districts in Saskatchewan we have no medical attention; people are thirty to fifty miles from the nearest doctor. This instance came to my attention this summer. In one of the reestablishment blocks, a mother was taken ill. In order to get her to a hospital the husband had first to see the relief officer. To do that, he had to travel some thirty miles. He went, got the order, came back, started to take the woman to the hospital, some thirty-five miles distant. They could not get in with a oar. This woman was the mother of ten children and was expecting another child. He loaded her in a wagon and started to take her out to where a car could he obtained. She took sick on the way; he

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
had to take her out on the side of the road, make a bed with some sheaves, the child was born there; he had to go home, get a manure boat with which he cleaned out his barn and take her back home on that manure boat. The child died; the mother is a cripple for life. In a country like Canada with our wealth and resources things like that are a disgrace. That is not an isolated instance. These conditions are a direct result of the prices that agriculture has been receiving in the prairie provinces for its products for the past ten years.
You do not have to go to the prairies for that; we have it in Ontario.

So much the worse. The present policy of the government with regard to the prices of grain is simply placing the grain growing industry of this dominion on relief. In effect, it says to western Canada: "You produce grain at less than cost. We know you cannot continue to do it, so to keep you from starving we will give you relief in the form of acreage bonus or summer-fallow bonus."
I have never believed in relief; I have always believed that the work and wage programme is to be preferred. We in this group were called visionaries in the years prior to the war when we suggested such a programme. We were told it wras impracticable, "Where would the money come from?" That sounds rather flat to-day, and I suggest that the present position of the government with regard to agriculture is just as weak. Agriculture does not want relief; what it wants is just what is being given to every other industry in this country, namely, a fair price for its products which will allow it to live and produce the food required for ourselves and for Great Britain in the increasing quantities that she desires. A price for our products in line with the costs we have to pay is essential to efficiency and increased production. Setting a maximum price below that point will certainly lead to decreased production.
In 1926-29 the average price for No. 1 butter, basis Montreal, was thirty-eight cents The average for the past year was considerably below that. Setting the price of butter last year at a level below the cost of production resulted in an increase in the export of dairy cattle to the United States in the first six months of this year of approximately 35 per cent. All this is taking place at a time when Great Britain is asking for more dairy products. We are deliberately forcing thousands of people out of agriculture and into industry. In the district from which I come, and all through Saskatchewan, there are thousands of sale bills displayed, and I believe the situation is the same in Ontario. Every farmer living on marginal
land or on land which has not been producing is being forced into industry. I should like to remind hon. members that when a dairy herd is disposed of, it cannot be replaced overnight; it requires from five to ten years of careful breeding. I feel certain that if present prices of agricultural products are maintained, within a year we shall be faced with a distinct shortage of dairy products in Canada, and Great Britain will still be asking for more of these commodities. In any agricultural paper in Ontario this belief will be seen stated time and again.
The actions of some of the boards and controls established by this government, for which the government alone must accept responsibility, have deliberately impeded the growth and development of the cooperative movement in Canada. This year our cooperative refinery in Regina has been unable to secure sufficient crude oil for its requirements and has had to buy large quantities of refined products from the regular oil companies while its own plant stood idle. The allotment of cars to the pools during the past year is another instance. As a result of this allotment, the handlings of the pool elevators have been reduced by approximately 40 per cent.
Finally, I should like to say that if this government are anxious to secure the cooperation of all classes and sections of this country in an all-out war effort, as they -wish it to appear, they have the remedy in their own hands. Let them consult labour and agriculture in the same manner that they consult industry to-day. Let them cut out the petty political patronage which is rampant throughout this country. Let them demonstrate byconcrete action that it is their intention to bring about real equality of sacrifice. We have heard platitudinous phrases coming from the Prime Minister and the Minister of Pensions and National Health. These are not enough. Here is what Hon. Ernest Bevin, who next to Mr. Churchill is the greatest leader of the British people to-day, has to say:
This war has taught us that never again can we be complacent; that it is not in platitudes or phrases that the world's solution of injustice, poverty, and social inequality can be solved, but in wise planning, thinking and action of the nations actuated by these motives.
That is what we need in Canada to-day, more action and less talk.

I should like to say just a word with regard to that paragraph of the order in council which is really the adjustment clause, and which has been so vigorously attacked by the hon. member for Lake Centre. To my mind that is the redeeming feature

I have received a number of complaints from farmers in western Canada respecting the arrangement with regard to instalment buying. It has been pointed out that it is impossible for those who receive their principal income from the sale of wheat

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
to meet payments on a monthly plan. Would the minister make a statement as to whether it is possible to have a 50 per cent down payment, and then have the balance paid next harvest, or a year from the time the purchases are made?
Automobiles are now a necessity in many areas of western Canada. Tractors, too, must be used. I understand they come under the regulations, and I should like the minister to make a statement respecting them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have received a number of representations similar to those of the hon. member, and I have forwarded them to the war-time prices and trade board. I am informed that the matter of the amendment of the regulations is under consideration at the present time. Perhaps I am not thoroughly acquainted with the principle underlying the monthly payments; but I should think that the important elements are, first, the size of the down payment and, secondly, the period within which the remainder of the price must be paid. If that is correct, there is an opportunity for some amendment to the present provision for monthly payments, without vitiating the principle of the order. The matter is under consideration.

My impression of the
regulations with respect to instalment buying is that they are not helpful to anyone, excepting the financing corporations. They shorten the time, but as far as I know, the commodity is not reduced in price for those buying on that basis. I believe when the time is shortened, and the financing corporations are given a better deal, it should be reflected in the benefit accruing to those who buy on the instalment plan. I do not know much about these matters, because I have not bought on instalments. In my view, however, that is a point which should be considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The object of the order in
council relating to instalment buying is not that of making it any easier for the purchaser to buy. The idea is to make it more difficult for him to buy.

But there should be no
objection to performing two functions at the same time, if it can be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The matter of price fixing or price control is separate altogether from the matter of t'he regulation of instalment buying. There was a tremendous amount of durable consumer goods being bought in Canada on the instalment plan. Small down payments were accepted; long periods were given for the completion of the payments, and people

were loading themselves up with obligations. They were buying goods which were using up valuable war materials. People were running into debt and making their futures very uncertain by entering into these long-term instalment contracts, and it was considered desirable to make the payments more strict. The objective there has nothing to do with the objectives of the price control regulations.

Has the minister given consideration to the effect of these price control regulations upon what is known as "loss leader" legislation in certain of the provinces? Some of the provinces have such legislation. In British Columbia in the last few years they have developed an act known as the Commodities Minimum Loss Act, the purpose of which is to prevent chain stores in particular from advertising certain goods at a rate below the cost to them, really using that method to sell their other products. Such a practice does not necessarily mean any benefit to the consumer and it was considered an unfair method of merchandising. The passing of this legislation brought about more orderly merchandising, and in the province it was considered a step in the right direction. The retail merchants now fear that these regulations will upset that legislation, the result being that retailers, large and small, will be brought back to the position in which they were some years ago. Regulation 5 (2) reads:
No such federal, provincial or other authority shall fix or approve any specific, minimum or maximum prices or markups in respect of any goods or services without the written concurrence of the board.
That would seem to be in direct conflict with the language of the British Columbia act, which states in section 3:
No retailer shall offer for sale, sell, or keep for sale in the province any grocery product at a price less than five per centum above the cost of the same to the retailer.
I believe there is a similar statute in Alberta.
I ask the minister to give the most careful consideration to the provincial legislation. The dominion regulations should not be such as to interfere with that act. These retailers are to be found in all our cities and towns and are generally the key men and women in their respective communities. I am convinced that they are only too anxious to cooperate in making this price control effective, and they can do it far better than any other class. I think this matter should be looked into, and the minister should make sure that these retailers do not lose their present position by virtue of the new regulations.

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall bring the hon. gentleman's representations to the attention of the board. Before I heard my hon. friend speak, I was not aware that there was any conflict between these regulations and the "loss leader" legislation of British Columbia.
Was it intended that there should be no conflict between these regulations and the "loss leader'' legislation of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that it was considered. There are provincial boards, such as milk boards, which fix minimum prices, and it was considered necessary to make sure that the war-time prices and trade board would have power to carry out its responsibilities regardless of the power vested in any local body. I think that was the situation which it was thought would be covered by that particular regulation. As I understand the hon. gentleman, he is suggesting that under the "loss leader" legislation of British Columbia it is illegal to sell below cost plus a certain mark-up, and that in that sense a minimum price is fixed by the legislation, whereas the regulation referred to by the -hon. gentleman provides that any fixing of minimum prices is subject to the written concurrence of the board.
That is what I am afraid of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not in a position to say that the board would give written concurrence. If the cost plus the mark-up brought the price above the ceiling, I suppose the board might not give its written concurrence, and to that extent there might be a conflict between the maximum price regulation and the "loss leader" legislation of British Columbia. I do not, however, think the regulation was framed with a view of enabling the board to break through that legislation. That is an accidental rather than an intentional result of the regulation.

I suggest that provincial legislation should be considered as being stronger than a regulation passed by a provincial board. When the act is working successfully in the province, I think it would be unwise to interfere with it by these price control regulations, certainly without giving the matter the most careful consideration.

There is one point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister in connection with the control of instalment buying. I refer to the sale of automobiles. In many ranching and farming districts the distance between the homes of the settlers and the market towns is considerable. Automobiles are needed, not for pleasure but to carry on the business of farming or ranching. The regulations provide that instalment payments shall be made at rather short intervals, whereas the average rancher or farmer has money at practically only one season of the year, when he sells his live stock or the product of his farm. Automobile dealers feel that this regulation will bring about a great change in their method of doing business and will prevent many people who need cars in their business from getting them. When this matter is being considered I hope that this situation will not be overlooked.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that the matter is being given consideration by the board at the present time.
Would the minister indicate by what method a price will be decided upon for a commodity which was not on sale in the period mentioned; for instance, asparagus next May?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to commit the board, but I think it is fair to say that there are certain seasonal fruits and vegetables which may be outside this order altogether. It may be impossible to make it apply to them. But that is a matter which will have to be dealt with by the board. I say that because it is obviously unfair to apply these regulations literally to certain fruits and vegetables which have a high value in one month, a very low value in another month, and perhaps had a very low value in the base period. I hope I am not saying anything which will be taken as a commitment or any intimation of what the board is going to do, because they must have complete freedom to work these things out themselves. But from the beginning it was thought that in the case of fruits and vegetables it might be necessary to go rather far in departing from the literal terms of the order.

I should like to support the view expressed by the hon. member for Melfort in connection with the controls which will be necessary. He mentions the attractive advertisements in newspapers urging people to buy certain commodities. I followed with a great deal of interest the minister's statement the other night and I entirely agree as to the evils of inflation, but I think even further controls are going to be necessary and I think they should be introduced.
I have before me the bureau of statistics' August, 1941, report of monthly sales of new motor vehicles in Canada, and I find that new motor vehicle sales in Canada during

The War-Finance-Price Ceiling
August, 1941, excluding deliveries to the government for war purposes, numbered 7,222 new vehicles, an increase of 45 per cent in number and 56 per cent in dollar value over August, 1940. There is also another report giving a comparison of retail sales in Canada for the period January to September, 1941, compared with the period January to September, 1940. and it contains some alarming figures. Boot and shoe stores have increased their sales by 18-5 per cent; candy stores, 18-4 per cent; men's clothing stores, 2T8 per cent; women's clothing stores, 19-4 per cent; department stores, 17-8 per cent; drug stores, 15-7 per cent; furniture stores, 14-4 per cent; grocerj' and meat stores, 14-1 per cent; hardware stores, 18 per cent; radio and electrical stores, 17-1 per cent; restaurants, 16-1 per cent; variety stores, 21-3 per cent.
A comparison of retail sales of boot and shoe stores and jewellery stores for September, 1940, and September, 1941, shows that in the maritime provinces boot and shoe stores have increased their sales by 19-1 per cent; jewellery stores, 43-8 per cent; Quebec, 17-9 and 21-2 per cent respectively; Ontario, 15-1 per cent and 24-5 per cent; prairie provinces, 19-3 per cent and 16-3 per cent; British Columbia, 16*2 and 44 per cent respectively.
These statistics indicate that the consumption of goods has proceeded at a very remarkable rate right across the country, and therefore I think that, in addition to the controls which the minister has outlined, it is going to be necessary to control the manufacture of these commodities. When one considers the need for mechanized equipment for the army, an increase of 45 per cent in the number of motor vehicles sold indicates that we have a very large number of workers and a large amount of material going into the production of these motor vehicles which are sold chiefly or to a very large extent for pleasure purposes and using material which should be devoted to war purposes.
I have here a very interesting article on " Economic Organization for Total War " by E. F. Penrose, economic adviser to the International labour office. I might mention to the committee that this is the international organization with head offices in Geneva until war broke out, which our government have been supporting financially. Mr. Penrose in his article discusses methods of restricting consumption, and says:
, There should be no reduction but an increase in the consumption of basic necessities by those who at present consume less of them than is required to maintain health and efficiency. Next, as regards the incomes of those who earn more 
than is required for the maintenance of health and efficiency, the higher the income the greater should be both the absolute and the proportionate reduction of the amount left available for consumption, up to a certain level above which no further income should be left for consumption.
I know that the minister considers he has gone a long way in increasing the income tax, but I feel that he will have to go a great deal further because people with large incomes are still left in the position where they can go into the market and buy luxury goods, thus forcing up the price level and creating a serious problem with which the minister will have to reckon. That will be in addition to the schemes he has so far devised.
Mr. Penrose goes on to discuss the different types of methods that can and should be followed. He mentions the rationing of consumer goods, and says:
Rationing of consumers' goods subject to w'ar scarcity is essential in communities in which income is unequally distributed, to ensure necessities to the lower income groups and to prevent hoarding and remove the need for queues.
Rationing of raw materials is also an effective weapon in the hands of the central government, for the purpose of controlling private business in war-time with a view to maximising the production of war goods and minimising the production of consumers' goods which can be foregoing with least injury to the public. This form of control is speedier and more direct than one based on fiscal and financial measures alone.
He goes on to examine the effect of taxes and loans on the distribution of the restriction of consumption among different income
groups, and says:
The distribution of the restriction of consumption has to be examined from the standpoints of equity and of the efficient conduct of the war. Voluntary loans have the advantage over compulsory loans and taxation, of facilitating adjustment between persons of similar incomes but different financial responsibilities and different future prospects. But they have the grave disadvantage of allowing less conscientious persons to continue a higher level of consumption than more conscientious persons; this is both inequitable and prejudicial to the conduct of the war.
Voluntary lending tends to produce unfavourable results on the distribution of income after the war, since high income groups are in a better position to save than low income groups.
Regarding taxation and social justice he
says:
First, incomes below the minimum amount necessary to purchase a specified standard of consumption goods should be exempted. Second, above this minimum the higher the income of the individual, the more should his previous consumption of goods and services be restricted. . . . On grounds of equity the entire amount of very large incomes above a certain point should be taken.

Gasoline
There are people in Canada who are not willing to accept that, but I should like to repeat that they are the people to whom Canada has been very kind; they have a great deal at stake and should be prepared for much higher income taxes. Mr. Penrose goes on to say:
The majority of economists have held that high income taxes do not reduce the efforts of business men, since the tax is only imposed on income actually received. However, this view has been criticized on the ground that high taxation diminishes net yields to invested funds and thus reduces the advantages of investing over holding cash idle. . . .
But on grounds of equity it cannot be claimed legitimately that customs and excise duties are the best means of restricting the consumption of things which produce harmful physical effects if consumed in excessive quantities.
Then he mentions the sales tax as unfair taxation, and says:
Financial policy should aim at preventing as far as possible price rises that give opportunities for excess profits, and excess profits should be subject to a one hundred per cent tax.
The argument that entrepreneurs will relax their efforts in war emergencies unless they are permitted to make large incomes in excess of the amount they pay in taxes implies that, as a class, business men are less willing than other sections of the community to make sacrifices to save the community in the hour of need.
As I said, I think the minister is going to have to go a great deal further than he has as yet gone. I realize that there are grave dangers in giving to a board the very wide powers which have been given, but the minister well stated the alternatives, and I think we should not be unduly concerned as long as those boards are appointed by governments which are elected in a democratic way, and as long as the elected representatives of the people have controls over those who are devising and enforcing the regulations. In a democracy, although members may be critical of government policies, we have to bow to the will of the majority and hope that those who have been granted very wide powers will use them in the best interests of the democracy, and to enable our democratic country to make its greatest contribution in this very critical time.
I submit this point of view to the minister because I anticipate that he will have a great deal of pressure from other groups who are going to be constantly complaining that these regulations interfere with profits. I imagine that representations are made by thousands of people who say, "We are not going to be able [DOT]to make the profits we formerly made." But sacrifices have to be made by all groups in the community in the present emergency, and
those best able to do so should make the greatest sacrifices.

May I ask the minister whether he believes that by December the firsl the board will be in a position to indicate fairly well their attitude, so that there will be some opportunity of planning for the future, as regards seasonal commodities such as fruits and vegetables?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think so, yes.

I believe that would relieve the situation.
